sections.html:
Explain a proposed behavioral mechanism and how evidence could test it, using a fresh hypothetical case and respecting the introduction’s lack of formal later-topic models.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources
  • R1: Define behavioral economics as specific psychological amendments with precise falsifiable predictions; give all five introductory directions.
  • R2: Distinguish the model/explanation question from the empirical-method question and classify the supplied illustration.
  • R3: Explain why an association or before/after sequence lacks the counterfactual needed for a causal conclusion; explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes without guaranteeing causality.
  • R4: Connect theory or intuition, evidence and application; frame a conditional prediction and state that the hypothetical example is not an actual result.

Finished-note locations:

  • What changes in a behavioral model
  • A field of questions and a method of evidence
  • Theory, evidence, and applications in this course

Use P002/V002/ingest 3 and O001-C1, objective revision 2. Supported instruction can use this block and linked notes. Independent acquisition and delayed attempts are closed note, with blank paper and pen only; no calculator, device, AI, hint or key exposure. Present only the question before the learner responds; keys remain teacher-side. Unknown help/access is unscorable for independence. Hypothetical inputs instantiate supported mechanisms and are not empirical findings.

Check the prerequisites

No prior course objective is required; the focused foundational diagnostic below establishes only entry conditions.

No prior course objective required. O001-P1 v1, foundational reading check: “A model predicts an action; an observation records an action. Which is a prediction and which is evidence?” Key: model statement is prediction; recorded action is evidence used to confront it. Pass only if both roles distinguished; partial if only one; fail if reversed. Repair: read Motivation, intuition, and definitions and explain the definition of falsifiable before proceeding. This check does not count as acquisition.

Entry checks have item version v1, and pass/partial/fail plus repair routes above. Their exact limited outcomes do not certify the upstream objective. A waiver requires actual committed compatible evidence, never familiarity or assumed mastery. If a diagnostic fails, use its named prepared explanation and support before continuing; do not cycle through full upstream independent items just to diagnose.
sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html:
A plausible story is not sufficient: the mechanism must generate a prediction that evidence could contradict. Behavioral economics concerns what explains choices; experimental economics concerns how evidence is generated. They can be used together. The five introductory directions are broader motivations, imperfect self-control, imperfect attention, inaccurate beliefs, and preferences that need not remain fixed. These are distinct amendments, not one universal claim of irrationality.

Visual support:

  • Introduction slide 06 correlation — inspected qualitative/source support; retrieve the finished note’s adjacent explanation.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Begin with a conventional model’s assumptions, then identify the precise proposed amendment. Fairness alters motivation; available but overlooked information concerns attention; incorrect perceptions concern beliefs. A planned but unimplemented choice concerns self-control; a change in motivation concerns preferences’ stability.
  2. Derive a conditional prediction from that amendment. A prediction must state an observable contrast and conditions under which it could be false. No formal equation for the later categories is supplied here.
  3. Ask separately how the evidence is obtained. Observing an undisturbed process preserves its natural setting, but association does not reveal what would happen if one variable changed while other relevant circumstances were controlled.
  4. A counterfactual is the outcome under an alternative situation. A before/after anecdote lacks a comparison for what would have happened without the intervention. Controlled information, incentives and context can move research closer to causal effects, but the introduction supplies no full identification design or estimator and no guarantee for every experiment.
  5. Use theory/intuition to generate the prediction, evidence to confront it, and an application to ask what a supported result would imply. The last step remains conditional until evidence exists.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Behavioral economics and experimental economics; fingerprint 31bef5277db2c184aebb25798e863489fbb1d3c09f0b61fe2fda9ccad0e8c3c1. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Behavioral economics and experimental economics

How should economics explain choices when people care about fairness, have difficulty following through on plans, overlook information, or hold inaccurate beliefs? Behavioral economics answers this question by changing particular assumptions about decision-making while retaining economic modeling and testable predictions. Week 1 introduces that approach and distinguishes it from experimental economics, the method used to gather much of the course's evidence. Introduction, PDF slides 2–3, 5–6

Return to the course's Week 1 section.

What changes in a behavioral model

Behavioral economics uses variants of traditional economic assumptions, often motivated by psychology, to explain and predict behavior and inform policy. The lecture also calls it psychology and economics or psychological economics. The word “behavioral” does not mean that other economists ignore behavior. It identifies the use of psychological insights, particularly cognitive psychology and social psychology, to improve assumptions about how people make choices. Introduction, PDF slide 2

The lecture presents this as amendments to traditional economics. Economic models still need precise, falsifiable predictions: predictions that evidence could show to be wrong. Broadening the assumptions is useful when it explains observed choices more accurately, rather than merely making a story sound plausible. Perfect rationality is one classical assumption that the lecture says need not be retained in every model. It does not claim that every traditional model fails or that mathematical modeling should be abandoned. Introduction, PDF slide 3

The lecture identifies five directions for amendments. They concern different parts of a decision, so they should not be collapsed into a single claim that people are “irrational.” The explanations below unpack the lecture's categories; the introduction does not yet provide their formal models. Introduction, PDF slide 3

Direction in the lecture What part of a choice it brings into view
Broader motivations: fairness, social preferences, group identity, social norms A person's motivation can include the treatment of others or expectations associated with a group, alongside their own material outcome.
Imperfect self-control Carrying out a plan can itself be difficult; an intended choice and a later action need not coincide.
Imperfect attention Information can be available without receiving the decision-maker's attention.
Inaccurate beliefs The decision-maker's view of the situation can differ from the relevant facts.
Preferences may not be fixed The motivations used to explain choices need not be treated as unchanging.

These categories organize later lectures rather than establish particular empirical results in Week 1. For example, a fairness explanation and an inaccurate-beliefs explanation change different elements of the model. Distinguishing them matters because a prediction or policy recommendation depends on the mechanism being proposed. This is a synthesis of the lecture's separate categories and its requirement of falsifiable predictions. Introduction, PDF slide 3

A field of questions and a method of evidence

Behavioral economics concerns the assumptions and explanations used to understand choices. Experimental economics is an empirical method that often tests those explanations. Calling an investigation experimental identifies how evidence is generated; it does not by itself identify the behavioral assumptions of the model being tested. The lecture deliberately separates the two terms. Introduction, PDF slide 5

Historically, economists often observed naturally occurring economic processes. Their advantage is that the processes can be studied in their undisturbed form. Their difficulty is causal interpretation: if two observed variables move together, that association alone does not tell us whether changing one would change the other. The lecture contrasts this with an experiment, where the researcher can control information, incentives, and context to estimate causal effects and investigate counterfactual scenarios. A counterfactual asks what would happen under an alternative situation, including one that did not occur in the naturally observed process. This explanation follows the contrast on slide 5; the slide does not specify a full identification strategy or an estimator. Introduction, PDF slide 5

The distinction matters when reading research. First ask which behavior the model seeks to explain and which assumption it changes. Then ask how the evidence allows the proposed explanation to be tested. An observed association may be informative without establishing the causal effect required by a policy argument. Experimental control offers a way to get closer to causal effects; the introduction does not say that every experiment automatically resolves every problem of interpretation. Introduction, PDF slides 5–6

The source's correlation-and-causation cartoon illustrates the caution. A person reports changing their belief after a statistics class. A second person treats that sequence as evidence that the class caused the change; the reply leaves that inference uncertain. The sequence is compatible with the causal explanation, but the cartoon gives no comparison showing what the person would have believed without the class. This is an interpretation of the displayed illustration, not a research result. Introduction, PDF slide 6

Theory, evidence, and applications in this course

The course's stated lecture sequence combines theory or intuition, evidence mostly from controlled experiments, and applications to issues such as rewarding employees, tackling poverty, and discrimination. Microeconomics I is the prerequisite because a learner needs the conventional framework with which to compare behavioral amendments. The organization and exam note records the study requirements and separates later-topic exam examples from the material taught here. Introduction, PDF slides 9–10

Agent-created illustration of the course's sequence: an investigation of how to reward employees can begin with a proposed motivation, derive a prediction about behavior under different incentives, and then ask whether evidence supports it. The lecture supplies the employee-reward application and the theory–evidence–application sequence. This illustration supplies no claim about an actual experiment, wage effect, or preferred policy. Introduction, PDF slide 9

Week 1 synthesis

Behavioral economics broadens assumptions about motivations, self-control, attention, beliefs, and preferences while requiring testable economic predictions. Experimental economics supplies a frequently used method for testing those predictions and estimating causal effects through control of the research environment. The two concepts answer different questions: what explains a choice, and how can evidence test that explanation? Detailed social-preference models and the later applications are outside this introductory material. Introduction, PDF slides 3, 5–6, 8–9

From the introduction to social preferences

The introductory categories above are developed further in the additional Social Preferences presentation. Ultimatum and dictator games provides the benchmark and laboratory patterns; Models of social preferences gives the utility functions and curve interpretation; Trust and cooperation games connects those motivations to surplus and cooperation. These pages extend the current Week 1 collection while preserving the scope of the original introductory material described here. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 12–14, 23, 37

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Two assumptions that the lecture brings into question; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Two assumptions that the lecture brings into question

The lecture contrasts broader motivations with two traditional assumptions. Selfish preferences make utility a function only of one's own payoff; without reputation-building, the benchmark does not add concern for another person's treatment or fairness. Exogenous preferences treat motivations as largely fixed traits, unresponsive to personal experiences or environmental factors. These are distinct claims: including another person's payoff changes the content of utility, while allowing preferences to respond to experience concerns where preferences come from. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 13

The presentation develops the first issue through payoff weights and behavior-dependent reciprocity. It does not estimate how preferences evolve over a lifetime or provide a formal preference-formation model. Its motivation is that social preferences can support cooperation and economic surplus, linked in the lecture to social capital. “Can” matters: some broader motivations, such as spite or negative reciprocity, also permit costly harm. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 13, 18–19, 22, 37

sections.html:
O001-W1 — A reward system

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Agent-created illustration: an employee-reward model adds concern about coworkers’ treatment; a researcher can compare incentive contexts; rewards and output are also naturally correlated.

Worked reasoning and result: The amendment is broader motivation. A possible conditional prediction is that choices differ across otherwise comparable incentive contexts if coworker treatment matters. This is a testable proposal, not an observed effect. Controlled contexts describe experimental economics; the motivation describes behavioral economics. Correlation alone cannot establish the effect of rewards because the alternative outcome under a different reward system is absent. Theory proposes the mechanism, evidence tests the prediction, and an employee-reward application follows conditionally. The other four directions are self-control, attention, beliefs and preference stability.

Checks and interpretation: Verify labels, active conditions, dimensions/signs where applicable and every source limitation before inferring a choice. This example is exposed instruction and cannot establish independence.
sections.title: Worked example

sections.html: Write your reasoning, then reveal the complete key to check each step.

interactions.prompt_html:
O001-S1 — A completion comparison

Item version: v1. Role: supported completion. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: Agent-created illustration: a poverty program presents available information. Complete: (a) name the behavioral category if information is overlooked, (b) distinguish explanation from controlled evidence, (c) say what a before/after improvement lacks, (d) list the other four directions and write a testable conditional prediction plus a conditional application. Hint allowed: begin with “If attention matters, then…”. Explain what experimental control contributes and why it does not automatically guarantee causal interpretation.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: (a) Imperfect attention. (b) The attention hypothesis is behavioral; controlling information/incentives/context is experimental. (c) The comparison for what would have happened without the program is absent; temporal order alone cannot identify causality. (d) Broader motivations, self-control, inaccurate beliefs, preferences not fixed. A prediction such as “If attention matters, making existing information salient changes choices in comparable contexts” is conditional and falsifiable; evidence would test it, and a program implication depends on that evidence. No program effect has been reported. Controlling information, incentives and context can move evidence closer to causal effects, but the introduction does not supply a complete identification design or guarantee that every experiment resolves every interpretation problem.

Support and rubric: Begin by letting the learner complete the specified steps using blank paper. Linked notes and up to two prepared hints are allowed here. Pass requires the essential component list with correct reasoning; partial means an incomplete component or isolated arithmetic slip, prompting the named repair; fail means a critical conceptual error. A correct supported answer permits fading help, never a claim of independent acquisition. After two ineffective hints show the needed step or pause.

interactions.prompt_html:
O001-I1 — independent acquisition

Item version: v1. Role: full_capability_check. Relation: near_transfer. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: A hypothetical employee overlooks available reward information. Explain behavioral economics, name the specific amendment and the other four directions; distinguish that explanation from a controlled comparison of information/incentives/context; assess the claim “reward information and output move together, so information caused output”; propose one falsifiable conditional prediction and trace theory–evidence–application while stating whether this is an actual result. Explicitly explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes, and why it does not automatically establish causality in every experiment.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: Behavioral economics amends specific assumptions with psychology while retaining precise falsifiable predictions. Overlooked information is imperfect attention; the remaining directions are broader motivations, self-control, inaccurate beliefs, preferences not fixed. The attention mechanism concerns explanation; a controlled comparison concerns experimental evidence. Association lacks the counterfactual and cannot alone show a causal effect; experimental control helps without automatically solving all interpretation. One accepted conditional prediction: if attention affects choices, making reward information salient changes choices in otherwise comparable settings. Theory proposes it; evidence tests it; reward-policy implications are conditional. This is an agent-created hypothetical, not a reported study.

Item rubric: All listed required components must be supplied, with correct reasoning and limits; apply the component decision rules in Rubric and independence. Conceptually equivalent explanations and exact fractions/consistent decimals are acceptable. No assistance, notes, calculator, device, AI or key access for an independent/delayed attempt; blank paper and pen only. C1 is a supported repair after scoring the original response and does not count toward acquisition or delayed retention.

interactions.prompt_html:
O001-I2 — independent acquisition

Item version: v1. Role: full_capability_check. Relation: near_transfer. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: A hypothetical decision-maker predicts another person’s action inaccurately. A natural record shows mistaken forecasts and poor choices together; another investigation controls information, incentives and context. Define the behavioral approach, identify its category and list the other four directions; classify explanation versus method; evaluate the causal claim from the natural record; give one falsifiable conditional prediction and a conditional application through theory–evidence–application. Explicitly explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes, and why it does not automatically establish causality in every experiment.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: Specific psychological amendments plus falsifiable economic predictions define the approach. Inaccurate beliefs is this category; others: broader motivations, imperfect self-control, imperfect attention, preferences not fixed. The belief hypothesis is behavioral economics; controlled evidence is experimental economics. Co-occurrence does not reveal the counterfactual causal effect; controls can help, not guarantee. Accepted prediction: if mistaken beliefs affect the choice, correcting the information changes choices in comparable contexts. Theory derives it, evidence confronts it, an information application remains conditional; no actual effect is established by this hypothetical.

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks
  • R1: Define behavioral economics as specific psychological amendments with precise falsifiable predictions; give all five introductory directions.
  • R2: Distinguish the model/explanation question from the empirical-method question and classify the supplied illustration.
  • R3: Explain why an association or before/after sequence lacks the counterfactual needed for a causal conclusion; explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes without guaranteeing causality.
  • R4: Connect theory or intuition, evidence and application; frame a conditional prediction and state that the hypothetical example is not an actual result.

Every I1, I2, D1, D2 and C1 question/key explicitly addresses all required components above. The sole acquisition route is two separate, distinct, fresh unassisted passes on I1 and I2 under the current criterion and compatible tuple. Worked/support/diagnostic/correction items and delayed items are not acquisition substitutes. No shorter question silently fills a missing component. The fixed practice inputs differ across W1/S1/I1/I2/D1/D2/C1; learning constants from the notes remain common where retrieval of those exact facts is the outcome.

Pass: all essential components, necessary reasoning, assumptions and interpretation limits are present, with accurate outputs. Accept equivalent wording, correct alternative algebra and exact fractions or consistent rounding that preserves inequalities/ties. Partial: a missing component or isolated arithmetic/transcription slip with valid conceptual setup; score before explaining the repair and do not count this attempt as a pass. Fail: wrong regime/role/sign, invalid incentive logic, replacing utility with monetary sum, treating hypothetical or descriptive data as identified results, or dropping a stated condition that changes the conclusion. For the orientation objective, replacing a printed restriction with an invented rule is a critical error. Unscorable: ambiguous prompt interpretation outside the key, unknown assistance/access/exposure, or unavailable source tuple. No numeric point scale or mastery result is fabricated.

An independent check is fresh only if neither its question nor key has already been exposed, including during earlier diagnostics or feedback. Teach records actual help/access conditions. Correct repetition of an exposed task cannot establish fresh independence. I1 and I2 are reserved for acquisition; D1/D2 are reserved for delayed retrieval.
sections.title: Rubric and independence

sections.html:
Sign: equating behavioral and experimental or saying all observations prove causes. Tentatively ask what assumption changed and how evidence was obtained. Correction: label the mechanism and method separately; identify the absent alternative outcome. Hint 1: “Which claim explains the choice?” Hint 2: “What would happen without the intervention?” Use fresh C1 after feedback; C1 is repair only.

A sign is a tentative hypothesis about the error until the learner’s reasoning supports it. Score the initial response before giving the corrective explanation or either hint. At most two ineffective hints, then show the specific prepared step or pause. After two unsuccessful full independent attempts, stop quizzing and use support/prerequisite repair; request new full variants from plan if needed.

O001-C1 — fresh correction only

Item version: v1. Role: correction_repair. Relation: near_transfer. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: Fresh repair: a hypothetical allocation model includes fairness; a natural record associates generous allocations and training, and controlled information/incentives/context are possible. Explain the behavioral approach, name the direction and other four, separate model and method, reject or qualify the causal inference, and propose a falsifiable conditional prediction with a theory–evidence–application chain. Explicitly explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes, and why it does not automatically establish causality in every experiment.

Key: Fairness changes broader motivations; the other four directions are self-control, attention, inaccurate beliefs and preferences not fixed. Psychological amendments must yield precise falsifiable economic predictions. Fairness explains choice; controlled contexts concern experimental evidence. The natural association supplies no counterfactual for generosity without training and cannot alone establish causality; controls help without guaranteeing it. A conditional fairness-based contrast in choices is acceptable as a hypothetical prediction, followed by testing evidence and a conditional allocation application. No actual training effect has been demonstrated.

Item rubric: All listed required components must be supplied, with correct reasoning and limits; apply the component decision rules in Rubric and independence. Conceptually equivalent explanations and exact fractions/consistent decimals are acceptable. No assistance, notes, calculator, device, AI or key access for an independent/delayed attempt; blank paper and pen only. C1 is a supported repair after scoring the original response and does not count toward acquisition or delayed retention.

sections.html: I1 and I2 are prepared above for immediate acquisition. Present each question without its key. This interval is a practical validity guard, not a personalized optimum. A delayed pass requires all current essential components. interactions.prompt_html:
O001-D1 — delayed independent retrieval

Item version: v1. Role: full_capability_check. Relation: near_transfer. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: A hypothetical learner intends to carry out a choice but later fails to do so. Their performance improved after a class, and a researcher proposes controlled contexts. Define behavioral economics, identify the direction and the other four; distinguish model from method; assess whether the class caused the improvement; supply a falsifiable conditional prediction and the theory–evidence–application chain with the evidence limitation. Explicitly explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes, and why it does not automatically establish causality in every experiment.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: The approach changes particular assumptions using psychological insight and retains falsifiable predictions. The intended/action gap is imperfect self-control; other directions: broader motivations, attention, beliefs and preference stability. The self-control account is a model explanation; controlled contexts are an empirical method. A before/after sequence lacks what performance would have been without class; it cannot alone establish causality. A conditional prediction linking implementation support to action in comparable contexts is acceptable if explicitly a hypothesis, not a taught empirical result. Theory proposes, evidence tests, application follows only conditionally; controlled evidence helps without a universal guarantee.

Item rubric: All listed required components must be supplied, with correct reasoning and limits; apply the component decision rules in Rubric and independence. Conceptually equivalent explanations and exact fractions/consistent decimals are acceptable. No assistance, notes, calculator, device, AI or key access for an independent/delayed attempt; blank paper and pen only. C1 is a supported repair after scoring the original response and does not count toward acquisition or delayed retention.

interactions.prompt_html:
O001-D2 — delayed independent retrieval

Item version: v1. Role: full_capability_check. Relation: near_transfer. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: A hypothetical person’s motivation varies across experiences rather than remaining fixed. A report associates those experiences with choices. Define the behavioral approach; name this amendment and all four others; distinguish it from experiments controlling incentives/information/context; assess the report’s causal interpretation; propose a falsifiable conditional prediction and trace theory–evidence–application without claiming a study result. Explicitly explain what controlling information, incentives and context contributes, and why it does not automatically establish causality in every experiment.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: Preference stability is the amendment; others are broader motivations, self-control, attention and inaccurate beliefs. Behavioral economics uses precise psychological amendments with falsifiable predictions; experiments describe evidence generation. Association lacks a counterfactual showing choices absent the experience; controls can move toward causal effects without a guaranteed full design. Accepted prediction: if this proposed motivation change matters, comparable choice contexts following different experiences yield different choices; it must remain explicitly hypothetical. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Write acceptance as \((M-r,r)\) and rejection as \((0,0)\). Compare the receiver’s own money last: \(r>0\) beats zero; at \(r=0\) both choices tie.
  2. The proposer anticipates this response and retains as much as feasible. “Next to nothing accepted” is the lecture benchmark. An exact zero or smallest positive offer requires the offer grid and a zero-offer tie rule. Whole units and rejection of zero imply offer 1; accepting zero permits offer 0. Do not invent a unique zero result without those assumptions.
  3. Remove the veto. DG now implements \((M-r,r)\) for any offer. A monetary maximizer chooses zero because \(M-r\) falls with \(r\); there is no receiver acceptance stage to anticipate.
  4. Lecture summaries: UG modal offer 40–50%; very few below 20%; offers below 20% often rejected more than 50%. DG more than 60% give positively and mean share is roughly 20%; received endowment versus earned changes giving, with earned giving diminishing but no supplied effect size. A modal amount, fraction of givers and mean share are different summaries. Empty polls give no additional results.
  5. Positive UG giving can insure against anticipated rejection; positive rejection sacrifices money and challenges the pure-money receiver benchmark. DG giving removes the veto explanation but does not isolate a unique preference. The lecture’s rates are approximate descriptive summaries, not universal individual choices or full causal estimates.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Ultimatum and dictator games; fingerprint 7fcbcf59c96d3145f48d169f3d0d67803d35906f7eb964956bb862de70dd5693. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Ultimatum and dictator games

Do people maximize only their own monetary payoff when choosing how to divide money? The ultimatum game and dictator game isolate different parts of this question. In the ultimatum game, the recipient can reject an allocation; in the dictator game, the recipient has no such power. Comparing them helps distinguish the effect of threatened rejection from willingness to give when rejection is impossible. Both are introduced as anonymous, incentivized laboratory decisions, rather than hypothetical evidence about what every person always does. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 2–3, 8–11

Return to Behavioral Economics — Week 1. The experimental-method distinction is developed in Behavioral and experimental economics.

The ultimatum game's sequence and payoffs

The ultimatum game (UG) has two players, a proposer and a receiver. The proposer is given a fixed monetary pie and chooses a split. The receiver then accepts or rejects. Acceptance implements the split; rejection leaves both players with nothing. The source specifies a one-time, anonymous interaction: the receiver does not know, and will not learn, the proposer's identity. Participants are paid according to their choices. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 2–3

Notation and payoff accounting unpacked from the setup: let \(M>0\) be the pie and \(r\in[0,M]\) the amount offered to the receiver. Acceptance gives monetary payoffs

\[(x_P,x_R)=(M-r,r),\]

where \(P\) labels the proposer and \(R\) the receiver. Rejection gives \((0,0)\). Thus an offer is not a completed transfer: the receiver has a veto. Rejecting a positive offer is costly to the receiver as well as the proposer. This opportunity to impose a cost is the central difference from the dictator game. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 3

The lecture's example uses \(M=\text{CZK }500\) and asks whether the receiver would accept offers of CZK 0, 1, 20, 100, 150, 200 or 250. The corresponding proposer shares are 500, 499, 480, 400, 350, 300 and 250. These are choice prompts, not observed decisions. The slides also ask for the receiver's minimum acceptable offer and the selfish-model prediction; the exported poll slides contain no responses or results. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3–7

Deriving the self-regarding benchmark

Self-regarding preferences make a player's utility depend only on that player's own monetary payoff. The benchmark also assumes the proposer expects the receiver to be self-regarding. To solve the sequential game, reason from the receiver's decision backward to the proposer's offer. This is the lecture's comparison with a subgame-perfect equilibrium: a strategy prediction that remains optimal at the later decision stage, including after an offer has actually been made. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 5, 8

For any \(r>0\), a purely monetary receiver gets \(r\) from accepting and zero from rejecting, so acceptance is strictly better. A proposer who anticipates this wants to retain as much as possible and offer next to nothing. The lecture summarizes the prediction as an almost-zero offer that is accepted. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 8

Qualification derived from the payoff comparison: at exactly \(r=0\), acceptance and rejection both give the receiver zero. Pure self-interest alone therefore leaves the receiver indifferent at zero. An exact minimum offer depends on the allowed monetary unit and how that tie is resolved. If whole CZK offers are allowed and zero would be rejected, the smallest strictly profitable accepted offer is CZK 1. If zero is accepted, offering zero can be optimal. The source supplies neither a tie rule nor a complete offer grid, so its “next to nothing” prediction should not be turned into an unconditional unique zero-offer result. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 7–8

Typical ultimatum results and what they challenge

The lecture reports that the modal offer—the most common offer—is 40–50% of the pie, with very few offers below 20%. Offers below 20% are rejected very often, more than 50% of the time in the stated summary. It says these patterns have been replicated many times and differ substantially from the self-regarding subgame-perfect prediction. These percentages are the lecture's reported typical laboratory patterns, not a class-poll result or a universal rate for every design and population. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 8

The rejection of a positive amount is particularly informative: the receiver gives up money to prevent the unfavorable split from being implemented. Social-preference models explain how concern about relative payoffs or treatment can make such an action attractive even though it reduces monetary income. The observed action challenges the purely monetary benchmark under the stated setup; it does not by itself identify one unique preference model. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 8, 20–22

A positive proposer offer is also not sufficient evidence of altruism. Reasoning from the game's veto: even a self-interested proposer can offer more when expecting a low offer to be rejected. The offer may reflect concern for the receiver, anticipation of costly rejection, or both. This is why the dictator game's removal of the veto is useful. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 8–9

The dictator game removes the receiver's veto

The dictator game (DG) also has a proposer and receiver and a fixed pie, but the proposer’s chosen split is simply implemented. The receiver is completely passive. There is no acceptance or rejection stage. With the same notation, the implemented monetary payoffs are \((M-r,r)\). A strictly self-regarding proposer therefore chooses \(r=0\), because every positive transfer directly reduces their own payoff and cannot avoid a receiver veto. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 9

The lecture describes a typical laboratory implementation with a $10 pie supplied by the experimenter, participants randomly assigned to proposer and receiver roles, and anonymity about individual decisions or pairings. The endowment is received rather than earned. These procedural features matter when interpreting what the comparison does and does not hold constant. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 9

The stated typical results are that more than 60% of participants transfer a positive amount, with a mean transfer of roughly 20% of the endowment. The fraction of people giving something and the average fraction of the pie given are different quantities: a 20% mean does not mean that 20% of participants give or that every giver transfers exactly 20%. For the stated $10 endowment, 20% is about $2 as an arithmetic illustration, not a separately observed result. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 11

The lecture stresses sensitivity to procedural details: when the endowment is earned rather than received from the experimenter, giving diminishes. It does not provide a numerical size for that reduction. Positive giving therefore supplies evidence against complete monetary selfishness for many participants in the described setting, while its level depends on the experimental procedure. It does not establish that all participants are unselfish or that these laboratory averages directly predict giving in every other setting. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 9, 11

Reading the two games together

Feature Ultimatum game Dictator game
Who chooses the split? Proposer Proposer
Can the receiver reject? Yes; rejection gives both zero No; the split is implemented
Self-regarding proposer benchmark Offer next to nothing that will be accepted Give zero
What positive giving can reflect Social concern and/or anticipated rejection Giving without a receiver veto
What the source reports Substantial offers and frequent rejection of very low offers Many positive transfers; giving sensitive to the endowment procedure

The comparison isolates the receiver's strategic power, while the lecture's reported results show that many choices need a broader account of motivation. The next step is to define what “broader” means: Models of social preferences separates altruism, spite, inequality aversion and reciprocity. Trust and cooperation games then examines settings where behavior can change the total monetary surplus, instead of only dividing a fixed pie. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 8–13, 23–24

O002-W1 — Veto comparison

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Hypothetical: pie 80 units, receiver offered 8. Contrast UG and DG; assume whole units and UG receiver rejects zero but accepts every positive offer.

Worked reasoning and result: UG acceptance gives \((72,8)\); rejection \((0,0)\). A selfish receiver strictly accepts \(8\); zero ties monetarily, so the extra tie rule matters. Given whole units and reject-zero, selfish proposer offers \(1\), receiving \(79\). DG receiver has no veto and proposer gives \(0\), receiving \(80\). Strategic UG giving can reflect fear of rejection; DG positive giving cannot avoid a nonexistent veto. The lecture’s UG modal \(40\text{–}50\%\) corresponds to a range of shares, not every person; DG \(>60\%\) positive givers and \(\sim 20\%\) mean are separate quantities, and earned giving diminishes without a stated amount.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Select \(w=\rho\) for \(x_1\ge x_2\), otherwise \(w=\sigma\). Then \(U_1=wx_2+(1-w)x_1=x_1+w(x_2-x_1)\). Equality yields \(U_1(x,x)=x\) from either expression, so the pieces meet.
  2. With \(0<\rho<1\) and \(\sigma<-\rho<0\), ahead utility is \(x_1-\rho(x_1-x_2)\) and behind utility \(x_1-(-\sigma)(x_2-x_1)\). The disparity amounts are nonnegative in their own regimes; both are penalties. Since \(-\sigma>\rho\), the behindness penalty per unit is larger. This does not remove the value of own income.
  3. Fix utility \(k\): \(wx_2+(1-w)x_1=k\). For \(w\ne1\), \(x_1=(k-wx_2)/(1-w)\), so with vertical \(x_1\) and horizontal \(x_2\) the slope is \(-w/(1-w)\). At zero weight it is horizontal; at \(0<w<1\) downward; at negative weight upward. At \(w=1\) only \(x_2\) matters and the curve is vertical. At \(w>1\) the own coefficient is negative and the usual positive-own-weight interpretation fails; algebra gives an upward slope. A positive weight alone does not imply the plotted downward shape.
  4. Selfishness: both weights 0. Altruism: both positive, sometimes \(0<\sigma<\rho\), with no universal upper bound imposed by the lecture’s general definition. Spite: both negative. Inequality aversion: ahead positive/behind negative with the taught stronger-penalty condition. Source figures are qualitative, not estimates.
  5. To decide between allocations calculate utilities; an unequal high-payoff pair may outrank a low equal pair. Costly UG rejection can be consistent with a sufficiently strong behindness penalty, but aggregate rejection does not identify each individual’s parameters.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage A piecewise utility function for two people; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

A piecewise utility function for two people

Let \(x_1\) be person 1's monetary payoff and \(x_2\) person 2's payoff, measured in the same monetary units. \(U_1\) describes person 1's preferences over the pair. The lecture presents the following example under the heading Charness and Rabin (2002):

\[U_1(x_1,x_2)= \begin{cases} \rho x_2+(1-\rho)x_1,& x_1\ge x_2,\\ \sigma x_2+(1-\sigma)x_1,& x_1<x_2. \end{cases}\]

The dimensionless parameter \(\rho\) weights the other person's payoff when person 1 is at least as well off; \(\sigma\) applies when person 1 is behind. The coefficient on one's own payoff is correspondingly \(1-\rho\) or \(1-\sigma\). The conditions refer to monetary payoffs, not to a comparison of the two people's utilities. The lecture supplies this simplified example; it is not a reproduction of the full cited paper. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 14–18, 20

Algebraic unpacking: when \(x_1\ge x_2\), write utility as \(x_1-\rho(x_1-x_2)\); when \(x_1<x_2\), write it as \(x_1+\sigma(x_2-x_1)\). At equality both expressions give \(U_1(x,x)=x\), so the pieces meet. Their slopes can differ at the equality line. Changing \(\rho\) or \(\sigma\) changes how person 1 trades off own income against the other person's outcome. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 14, 20–21

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage How to read the indifference curves; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

How to read the indifference curves

An indifference curve joins payoff pairs giving the same utility to person 1. In the source figures the vertical axis is \(x_1\) and the horizontal axis is \(x_2\). The gray diagonal marks equal monetary payoffs. Do not reverse the axes when interpreting the curve's slope. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 15, 17, 19, 21

Within either regime, let \(w\) stand for its active weight, \(\rho\) or \(\sigma\), and fix utility at \(k\). Derived from the displayed function, for \(w\ne1\),

\[w x_2+(1-w)x_1=k \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_1=\frac{k-wx_2}{1-w}, \qquad \frac{dx_1}{dx_2}=-\frac{w}{1-w}.\]

With \(w=0\) the curve is horizontal. With \(0<w<1\) it slopes downward: more income for person 2 can compensate for less own income. With \(w<0\) it slopes upward: when the other person's gain lowers utility, own income must rise to compensate. These slope descriptions use the source figures' positive own-payoff coefficient. The lecture's general positive-weight statement does not itself impose an upper bound on every altruistic weight; if \(w=1\), own payoff drops out and the curve is vertical, while \(w>1\) changes the own-payoff sign. These boundary cases are algebraic qualifications, not additional empirical claims. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 14–19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Selfishness, altruism and spitefulness; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Selfishness, altruism and spitefulness

Selfish preferences

Setting \(\rho=\sigma=0\) gives \(U_1=x_1\). The other person's monetary payoff has no direct effect on person 1's utility. This is the benchmark used to solve the anonymous games by monetary incentives alone. A horizontal indifference curve means that any \(x_2\) is equally attractive when \(x_1\) is unchanged; the upward arrow in the source shows preference for more own income. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 15

Source slide 15: own payoff is vertical, the other person's payoff horizontal. With both social weights zero, the horizontal curves preserve own payoff, and higher curves are preferred. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 15

Altruism

The lecture calls \(\rho>0\) and \(\sigma>0\) pure altruism: the other person's payoff enters utility positively whether person 1 is ahead or behind. It sometimes adds \(0<\sigma<\rho\), meaning greater weight on the other person when that person has less than one's own payoff. In that case, the weight changes at equality even though both weights remain positive. Do not confuse the larger ahead-regime weight with a negative behind-regime weight. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 16–17

Source slide 17: downward-sloping segments show willingness to trade own income against the other person's income in the plotted positive-own-weight case. A change of slope at the equality diagonal represents different weights across the two regimes. The figure supplies no numerical parameter estimate. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 17

Spitefulness

For spiteful preferences, \(\rho<0\) and \(\sigma<0\). Increasing the other person's payoff while holding one's own fixed lowers utility in either regime. This is different from being selfish: a selfish person is indifferent to that change, while a spiteful person dislikes it. The own-payoff coefficient is then greater than one, and the indifference segments slope upward. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 18–19

Source slide 19: upward-sloping curves show that a higher other-person payoff requires extra own income to maintain utility. The preference arrow points toward more own income and less income for the other person; the gray equality line locates the payoff regimes. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Inequality aversion changes sign across equality; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Inequality aversion changes sign across equality

Inequality aversion dislikes disparities between own and another person's monetary payoff. The lecture labels its discussion Fehr and Schmidt (02) and specifies

\[0<\rho<1,\qquad \sigma<0,\qquad \sigma<-\rho<0.\]

When person 1 is ahead, the positive \(\rho\) means that increasing the poorer person's payoff at fixed own income reduces the disparity and raises utility. When person 1 is behind, the negative \(\sigma\) means that increasing the richer person's payoff at fixed own income widens the disparity and lowers utility. The last inequality says \(-\sigma>\rho\): the disadvantageous-inequality penalty is stronger than the advantageous-inequality penalty. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 20–21

The rewritten function makes the penalties explicit:

\[U_1= \begin{cases} x_1-\rho(x_1-x_2),&x_1\ge x_2,\\ x_1-(-\sigma)(x_2-x_1),&x_1<x_2. \end{cases}\]

This is derived from the source's function, not an extra estimated model. The first penalty subtracts a fraction of the amount by which person 1 is ahead; the second subtracts a positive weight times the amount by which person 1 is behind. The model still values own income. It does not imply that any equal allocation is always preferred to every unequal allocation regardless of the amount of money involved. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 14, 20–21

Source slide 21: each curve slopes down in the ahead region above the equality diagonal, then up in the behind region below it. The kink reflects a change from positive to negative weight on the other person's payoff. Higher-own-payoff curves represent higher utility; the picture is qualitative, not an estimate of the two penalty parameters. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 21

This distinction helps interpret ultimatum rejection: a receiver may prefer both players receiving zero to accepting a strongly disadvantageous positive split if the inequality penalty is sufficiently large. The relevant comparison is utility, not only money. Whether rejection occurs depends on the person's parameters and offered allocation; the lecture's aggregate rejection rates do not identify those parameters for each individual. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 3, 8, 20–21

O003-W1 — Two regimes and curves

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Hypothetical \(\rho =1/4,\sigma =-1/2\). Calculate \(U\) at \((80,40),(30,90),(40,40)\), slopes, and compare \((80,40)\) with equal \((40,40)\).

Worked reasoning and result: Ahead:\(80-(1/4)40=70\). Behind:\(30-(1/2)60=0\). Equal \(40\). Slopes ahead \(-(1/4)/(3/4)=-1/3\); behind \((1/2)/(3/2)=1/3\). Both penalties subtract disparities; behind rate \(1/2\) exceeds \(1/4\). Unequal utility \(70\) exceeds equal \(40\). At \(w=0\) horizontal,\(w=1\) vertical,\(w>1\) own coefficient negative; only \(0<w<1\) slopes down. Selfish \(\rho=\sigma=0\), altruistic both positive, spite both negative, taught inequality \(\rho\in(0,1)\),\(\sigma<-\rho\). No parameters estimated.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. In the displayed reciprocity equation define \(w(q)=\rho+\theta q\): utility is \(w(q)x_2+[1-w(q)]x_1\). Kindness gives \(w_+=\rho+\theta\), misbehavior \(w_-=\rho-\theta\), so \(w_+-w_-=2\theta>0\).
  2. Negative total weight after misbehavior requires \(\rho-\theta<0\), equivalently \(\theta>\rho\). A positive \(\theta\) alone cannot establish hostility; baseline \(\rho\) can be larger. At \(\theta =\rho\) the negative-treatment weight is zero.
  3. Identical allocations can have different utilities because \(q\) changes; this differs from unconditional altruism and inequality-only weighting. Do not say kindness raises utility for every fixed allocation: \(U_+-U_-=2\theta(x_2-x_1)\), so the sign depends on relative monetary payoffs. This is direct unpacking of the supplied equation, not an estimated treatment effect.
  4. As the notes’ labelled illustration, set both earlier payoff weights to \(1/2\): \(U=(x_1+x_2)/2\). Ranking this particular utility is equivalent to ranking the total. This supplies an illustration of efficiency concern within the existing function, not a complete separately estimated efficiency-seeking model or evidence that all efficiency preferences use these weights.
  5. Sequential trust lets a trustee observe the prior transfer; simultaneous cooperation requires a belief about current kindness before either action is seen. The lecture names positive reciprocity plus belief in cooperation but gives no separate quantitative simultaneous mechanism, measured intention rule, study rate or belief threshold. A single transfer cannot isolate the motivation.

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Reciprocity responds to prior treatment; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Reciprocity responds to prior treatment

Reciprocity means kindness toward someone who acted kindly and hostility toward someone who acted unkindly. The source adds \(q=1\) for person 2's kind action and \(q=-1\) for misbehavior, with sensitivity \(\theta>0\):

\[U_1(x_1,x_2)=(\rho+\theta q)x_2+(1-\rho-\theta q)x_1.\]

Define the effective social weight \(w(q)=\rho+\theta q\). A kind action gives \(w(1)=\rho+\theta\); misbehavior gives \(w(-1)=\rho-\theta\). Thus treatment changes the weight on the other person's payoff by \(2\theta\) between these two states. A negative response weight follows if \(\theta>\rho\); \(\theta>0\) alone does not ensure that the total weight becomes negative. These comparisons unpack the supplied equation. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 22

Reciprocity therefore differs from unconditional altruism and from payoff inequality alone. Two identical monetary allocations can have different utility if prior treatment changes \(q\). The lecture defines the two kindness states but supplies no detailed rule for measuring perceived intentions or estimating \(\theta\). The displayed equation is a simple illustration, not a full solution of every strategic game or a replacement of the earlier two-regime function in all contexts. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 22, 27, 36

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Efficiency-seeking and the welfare connection; fingerprint a396884c8a7d4f0e18bd39c4f58b861609e05785148d4187d07a3da9db9c548c. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Efficiency-seeking and the welfare connection

The lecture names efficiency-seeking alongside the other social preferences and lists it as a possible reason for trustor transfers. Its relevant intuition is concern for the total monetary surplus that cooperation can create. The presentation does not give a separate complete efficiency-seeking utility function or identify it from one observed transfer. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 12, 27, 35, 37

Agent-created illustration using the displayed model: \(\rho=\sigma=1/2\) yields \(U_1=(x_1+x_2)/2\), so maximizing this particular utility is equivalent to maximizing total monetary payoff. This illustrates how the existing payoff weights can value a larger total; it is not a claim that the lecture estimates those parameters or that all efficiency-seeking preferences take this exact form. Concern about totals, distribution and kind treatment can produce similar choices in some games, making the experimental comparison important. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 14, 27

Trust and cooperation games develops the distinction between splitting a fixed pie and expanding monetary surplus. Social preferences can encourage the latter, while beliefs and incentives still determine whether cooperation occurs. The central result of these models is a set of distinct mechanisms—positive payoff weights, negative payoff weights, disparity penalties and treatment-dependent weights—not a single universal “unselfish” preference. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 23–24, 35–37

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Reciprocity needs an expectation about the other player; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Reciprocity needs an expectation about the other player

The lecture's second explanation is positive reciprocity combined with the belief that the other person will cooperate. It cites Dawes and Thaler (1988) beside the observation that cooperation occurs even with a finite number of interactions, sometimes only once; the uploaded slide does not supply the underlying study design, sample, or numerical cooperation rate. Positive reciprocity means wanting to respond kindly to perceived kindness. In a simultaneous game there is no observed current action to reciprocate at the moment of choice, so an expectation about the other's cooperation is part of this proposed explanation. The lecture does not specify a separate payoff formula or a quantitative belief threshold for this mechanism. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 36

This differs from the trust game, where the trustee observes the initial transfer before returning money. It also differs from the unconditional warm-glow premium: a desire to reward kindness depends on how the other player's behavior is perceived or expected. The reciprocity model makes this dependence explicit. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 22 Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 36; connection between games

O004-W1 — Treatment shifts weight

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Hypothetical \(\rho =1/5,\theta =3/10\), allocation \((40,20)\); compare \(q\) states and efficiency illustration \((24,24)\) versus \((30,26)\).

Worked reasoning and result: Kind weight \(.5\),unkind \(-.1\),change \(.6\); \(U_{\mathrm{kind}}=.5(20)+.5(40)=30\), \(U_{\mathrm{unkind}}=-.1(20)+1.1(40)=42\). Negative after misbehavior since \(\theta >\rho\); kindness raises other-weight but lowers this fixed allocation’s utility because \(\text{own}>\text{other}\). Fixed altruism/inequality do not respond to \(q\). Efficiency illustration utilities \(24\) and \(28\), prefers larger total \(56\). It is not a separate efficiency model or motive identification; simultaneous reciprocity requires expectations whereas trustee sees transfer, no quantitative mechanism supplied.

Checks and interpretation: Verify labels, active conditions, dimensions/signs where applicable and every source limitation before inferring a choice. This example is exposed instruction and cannot establish independence.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

sections.html:
Signs: \(\theta >0\) automatically produces a negative weight; kindness always increases utility; half-total illustration called the complete efficiency model. Correction: calculate \(\rho -\theta\) and distinguish weight change from utility change; retain the illustration label and model limits. Hint1: subtract \(\theta\) from baseline \(\rho\). Hint2: multiply the weight change by \(x_2-x_1\). C1 is repair only.

A sign is a tentative hypothesis about the error until the learner’s reasoning supports it. Score the initial response before giving the corrective explanation or either hint. At most two ineffective hints, then show the specific prepared step or pause. After two unsuccessful full independent attempts, stop quizzing and use support/prerequisite repair; request new full variants from plan if needed.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Trustor starts with \(X\), sends \(Y\) in \([0,X]\); trustee receives \(\alpha Y\) and returns \(Z\) in \([0,\alpha Y]\), with \(\alpha >1\) dimensionless. Trustor payoff \(X-Y+Z\) counts retained cash plus return; trustee payoff \(\alpha Y-Z\) counts receipt less return.
  2. Add payoffs: \(X-Y+Z+\alpha Y-Z=X+(\alpha -1)Y\). \(Z\) cancels because redistribution changes shares, not total. Relative to initial \(X\), surplus is \((\alpha-1)Y\); \(Y=X\) maximizes this monetary sum. No separate cost is in these rules, and utility/distribution need not improve for every player.
  3. Start last: a self-regarding trustee maximizes \(\alpha Y-Z\) by \(Z=0\) after every feasible \(Y\). Anticipating this, a self-regarding trustor chooses \(Y=0\) to maximize \(X-Y\). This specifies optimal continuation even off equilibrium; both self-regarding preferences and expectations are required.
  4. An actual hypothetical trustor’s net gain is \(Z-Y\). Break-even needs \(Z=Y\). If a return proportion is explicitly \(Z/(\alpha Y)\), break-even proportion is \(1/\alpha\). The lecture’s \(\sim 33\%\) back has no defined denominator or aggregation. Only conditionally, with \(\alpha=3\) and exact one-third of multiplied receipt, \(Z=Y\) and gain \(0\); rounded \(.33\) gives \(Z=.99Y\),approximately zero. Do not infer actual individual-average returns by multiplying separately reported averages. The lecture also says about \(45\%\) of endowment sent; empty polls add no results.
  5. Initial \(Y\) can reflect repayment beliefs, altruism or efficiency concern; \(Z\) may reflect reciprocity but no unique motive follows from one action. Table \(35\) countries separates study count, sample size, fraction sent and proportion returned. US \(46\) studies/\(4552\) observations/\(.51\)/\(.34\); South Korea \(1\)/\(52\)/\(.67\)/\(.29\); Vietnam \(2\)/\(194\)/\(.33\)/n/a. n/a is missing, not zero. No visible table author/year, pooling/sampling/design controls, uncertainty or precise return denominator; it cannot establish causal country effects, national rankings or significance.

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The trust game: creating a surplus before deciding its division; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The trust game: creating a surplus before deciding its division

The trustor, also called the investor, starts with a monetary endowment \(X\). The trustor first chooses a transfer \(Y\), with \(0\leq Y\leq X\). The transfer is multiplied by a factor \(\alpha>1\) before reaching the trustee, also called the agent. The trustee then chooses a back-transfer \(Z\), with \(0\leq Z\leq\alpha Y\). Thus the trustee can return none, some, or all of the multiplied receipt. The interaction occurs once. Here \(\alpha\) denotes the lecture's multiplication factor; it is dimensionless, while \(X,Y,Z\) use the same monetary units. The final monetary payoffs are

\[x_{\mathrm{trustor}}=X-Y+Z, \qquad x_{\mathrm{trustee}}=\alpha Y-Z.\]

The trustor keeps the uninvested amount \(X-Y\) and receives \(Z\); the trustee keeps the multiplied receipt after subtracting the return. The lecture calls \(Y\) trust and \(Z\) trustworthiness. These names describe choices in this experimental game; interpreting the choices as pure measures of one underlying motive requires further care. The lecture presents the setup as a simplified principal–agent problem: an investor creates an opportunity for an agent, whose subsequent action determines whether the investor recovers the investment. Its analogy to commission-taking or stealing is an interpretation of the payoff arrangement, rather than an additional enforced contractual rule. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 24

Agent unpacking of the lecture's payoff equations: adding the two payoffs gives

\[\begin{aligned} x_{\mathrm{trustor}}+x_{\mathrm{trustee}} &=(X-Y+Z)+(\alpha Y-Z)\\ &=X+(\alpha-1)Y. \end{aligned}\]

The back-transfer \(Z\) cancels because it redistributes existing money between the players. The initial transfer creates a joint monetary surplus \((\alpha-1)Y\) because the experimental rules multiply it. Since \(\alpha>1\), a larger \(Y\) raises their combined monetary payoff, and \(Y=X\) maximizes that sum within this setup. This is the sense in which cooperation can create surplus. A larger monetary sum does not by itself establish that each player's utility rises: distribution and the players' preferences still matter. The calculation uses the game's stated multiplication rule and includes no separate production cost. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 24; algebraic interpretation

The self-regarding prediction by backward induction

The lecture attributes the first experimental implementation to Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe (1995), using \(X=\$10\) and \(\alpha=3\). It asks for a subgame-perfect equilibrium, an equilibrium in which the prescribed choices remain optimal in every continuation of the game, including continuations that would not occur on the equilibrium path. The classroom poll on PDF p. 26 contains a question, but the supplied file displays no poll results. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 25–26

Under the lecture's benchmark, both players maximize their own monetary payoff and the trustor expects the trustee to do so. Agent unpacking: start with the last decision. For any positive \(Y\), the trustee's payoff \(\alpha Y-Z\) decreases one-for-one with \(Z\), so the trustee chooses \(Z=0\). Anticipating this, the trustor expects \(X-Y\), which is maximized at \(Y=0\). With no initial transfer, the trustee's feasible return is also zero. The prediction is therefore no initial transfer and no return, despite the potential joint surplus. The logic requires the self-regarding preferences and corresponding expectations; it is not a prediction for every possible preference model. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 27

Observed transfers and what they reveal

The lecture reports that most studies find about 45% of the endowment sent and around 33% transferred back, characterizing the latter as around zero return to trust. These are the lecture's approximate summary figures, not results from the empty classroom poll or from one identified sample. PDF p. 27 does not explicitly define the denominator of the 33% figure. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 27

Conditional agent interpretation: if the return proportion means \(Z/(\alpha Y)\), then returning exactly one third of the trustee's receipt when \(\alpha=3\) gives \(Z=Y\). The trustor ends with \(X-Y+Y=X\), a zero net monetary gain on the investment, while a positive initial transfer still creates a joint surplus. Using the rounded value 0.33 gives \(Z=0.99Y\), approximately the same conclusion. This explains how the lecture's phrase can be consistent with its example, but it does not resolve the unspecified denominator. If 33% instead meant a proportion of the original endowment or of \(Y\), the calculation would differ. Nor can multiplying separately reported averages reconstruct an average individual investment return without the underlying data. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 27; conditional calculation

The lecture typically attributes back-transfers to reciprocal preferences: the trustee responds to the trustor's prior action. Initial transfers can reflect beliefs that the trustee will return money, altruism toward the trustee, or a concern for increasing the joint payoff. A positive \(Y\) therefore does not uniquely identify a belief in repayment, and a back-transfer alone does not identify reciprocity separately from every other possible motivation. The game's role is to make these motivations visible and distinguish its behavior from the stated selfish benchmark. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 27

Reading the cross-country table

Full source slide: Table 3, “Descriptive statistics by country,” lists 35 countries, the number of studies, total sample size, average fraction sent, and average proportion returned. The image preserves every country row and the missing return entry for Vietnam. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 28

The columns separate evidence quantity from transfer behavior. For example, the United States row reports 46 studies, a total sample of 4,552, an average fraction sent of 0.51, and an average proportion returned of 0.34. South Korea reports one study and 52 observations, with 0.67 sent and 0.29 returned. Vietnam reports two studies, 194 observations, 0.33 sent, and “n/a” for returned. The missing entry is not a zero. The table visibly shows variation in reported transfers and very different amounts of evidence across rows. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 28, table rows and headings

Source limitation: this slide supplies no author/year attribution for Table 3, sampling or pooling procedure, experimental-design controls, uncertainty intervals, or explicit denominator for the return column. The earlier citation to the original trust-game experiment does not establish the provenance of this later table. These descriptive averages therefore support a comparison of the displayed observations; they do not establish a causal effect of country, a representative ranking of national trust, or statistical significance of any difference. No underlying studies or external references were consulted to fill those gaps. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 28; interpretation limits

sections.html:
O005-W1 — Expansion versus division

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Agent-created hypothetical: \(X=12, \alpha =3, Y=4, Z=4\). Calculate payoffs, total, surplus and private gain; solve the monetary benchmark and interpret the lecture summary/table.

Worked reasoning and result: 1. The trustor keeps \(12-4\) and receives \(4\), ending with \(12\). The trustee receives \(3\times 4\) and returns \(4\), ending with \(8\). 2. Total is \(20=X+2Y\); surplus is \(8\); trustor net gain \(Z-Y\) is zero. 3. A self-regarding trustee returns \(Z=0\) after every \(Y\); anticipating this, the self-regarding trustor chooses \(Y=0\). 4. \(Y=X\) maximizes the monetary sum, without ensuring both utilities rise. 5. The lecture reports about \(45\%\) sent and about \(33\%\) returned, with the return denominator/aggregation undefined. Only if the proportion is \(Z/(3Y)=1/3\) does \(Z=Y\) imply zero gain; \(0.33\) gives \(0.99Y\) and approximately zero gain. Products of separate empirical averages cannot reconstruct individual mean returns. 6. Sends may reflect repayment beliefs, altruism or efficiency; returns may reflect reciprocity without identifying one motive. The US row is \(46\) studies, \(4,552\) observations, \(.51\) sent, \(.34\) returned; South Korea is \(1\), \(52\), \(.67\), \(.29\); Vietnam is \(2\), \(194\), \(.33\), n/a. Missing is not zero. These descriptive rows lack author/year, sampling/pooling/design controls, uncertainty and an explicit return denominator, so they establish no causal country effect, representative national ranking or statistical significance.

Checks and interpretation: Verify labels, active conditions, dimensions/signs where applicable and every source limitation before inferring a choice. This example is exposed instruction and cannot establish independence.

interactions.prompt_html:
O005-S1 — Complete cash accounting

Item version: v1. Role: supported completion. Required components: R1, R2, R3, R4.

Question: Agent-created hypothetical: \(X=18, \alpha =3, Y=6, Z=2\). Fill retained cash, receipt, payoffs, total, surplus, net gain, break-even return/proportion and selfish benchmark. Explain the lecture percentages, motive alternatives and US/Korea/Vietnam table limits. Hint 1: trace the return between players. Hint 2: cancel \(Z\) when adding payoffs. State the one-shot roles/sequence, general transfer constraints and units before interpreting the arithmetic.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: Retained cash is \(12\) and multiplied receipt is \(18\). Trustor payoff is \(14\); trustee payoff is \(16\); total is \(30\); surplus is \(12\); gain is \(-4\). General payoffs are \(X-Y+Z\) and \(\alpha Y-Z\), totaling \(X+(\alpha -1)Y\). Break-even return is \(Z=Y=6\); the proportion is \(1/3\) only when its denominator is the multiplied receipt. The selfish trustee returns zero after every feasible \(Y\), so the anticipating trustor sends zero. \(Y=X\) maximizes total money, not necessarily each utility. The lecture percentages are approximately \(45\%\) sent/\(33\%\) returned, with missing return denominator and aggregation. Exact one-third of the \(\alpha =3\) receipt implies zero net gain; \(.33\) gives approximately zero; multiplying separate empirical averages is unjustified. Initial transfers may reflect repayment beliefs, altruism or efficiency; returns may reflect reciprocity, without unique motive identification. US \(46\)/\(4552\)/\(.51\)/\(.34\), Korea \(1\)/\(52\)/\(.67\)/\(.29\) and Vietnam \(2\)/\(194\)/\(.33\)/n/a separate study/sample quantities from transfer means. n/a is missing. Absent table author/year, sampling/pooling/design, uncertainty and return denominator prevent causal country rankings or significance claims. General rules: \(X>0, \alpha >1, 0\le Y\le X, 0\le Z\le \alpha Y\); \(\alpha\) is dimensionless, and \(X\)/\(Y\)/\(Z\) share monetary units. The trustor/investor chooses first, then the observing trustee/agent chooses the return; there is one interaction.

Support and rubric: Begin by letting the learner complete the specified steps using blank paper. Linked notes and up to two prepared hints are allowed here. Pass requires the essential component list with correct reasoning; partial means an incomplete component or isolated arithmetic slip, prompting the named repair; fail means a critical conceptual error. A correct supported answer permits fading help, never a claim of independent acquisition. After two ineffective hints show the needed step or pause.

Solve the pure-money continuation benchmark with its expectation assumption and explain why a maximum monetary sum need not improve both utilities. Retrieve the lecture’s approximate transfer percentages, show the conditional \(\alpha =3\) one-third/rounded .33 arithmetic and explain denominator/aggregation limits. Distinguish possible motives and interpret the supplied US/Korea/Vietnam rows, table columns, missing entry and absent methods. Supplied source-table excerpt (Studies / Sample / Average fraction sent / Average proportion returned): US 46 / 4552 / .51 / .34; South Korea 1 / 52 / .67 / .29; Vietnam 2 / 194 / .33 / n/a. Read the displayed averages descriptively and explain which population-trait, causal or significance claims these data do not establish; no memorization of study/sample counts is required.
interactions.solution_html:
Key: General constraints are \(X>0, \alpha >1, 0\le Y\le X\) and \(0\le Z\le \alpha Y\); \(\alpha\) is dimensionless and \(X\)/\(Y\)/\(Z\) use the same monetary units. The trustor/investor chooses \(Y\) first in \([0,20]\); the trustee/agent observes it and chooses \(Z\) in \([0,24]\). The interaction occurs once. Payoffs are \(X-Y+Z=18\) and \(\alpha Y-Z=18\); total is \(X+(\alpha -1)Y=36\); surplus is \((\alpha -1)Y=16\); private gain is \(Z-Y=-2\). sections.title: Practice with fading assistance

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks
  • R1: State sequential roles, feasible \(X\)/\(Y\)/\(Z\) and \(\alpha >1\), derive both final monetary payoffs and cancellation of \(Z\) in total surplus.
  • R2: Derive selfish trustee zero after every transfer and anticipating trustor zero; distinguish joint monetary maximum from each player’s utility.
  • R3: Compute supplied hypothetical payoffs and break-even; retrieve lecture \(45\%\) sent/\(\sim 33\%\) back with undefined denominator/aggregation, only conditional \(\alpha=3\) one-third interpretation and no product-of-averages inference.
  • R4: Distinguish repayment belief/altruism/efficiency and possible reciprocity without uniquely identifying motives; read country columns/descriptive differences, missing Vietnam n/a and absent provenance/design/uncertainty controls.

Every I1, I2, D1, D2 and C1 question/key explicitly addresses all required components above. The sole acquisition route is two separate, distinct, fresh unassisted passes on I1 and I2 under the current criterion and compatible tuple. Worked/support/diagnostic/correction items and delayed items are not acquisition substitutes. No shorter question silently fills a missing component. The fixed practice inputs differ across W1/S1/I1/I2/D1/D2/C1; learning constants from the notes remain common where retrieval of those exact facts is the outcome.

Pass: all essential components, necessary reasoning, assumptions and interpretation limits are present, with accurate outputs. Accept equivalent wording, correct alternative algebra and exact fractions or consistent rounding that preserves inequalities/ties. Partial: a missing component or isolated arithmetic/transcription slip with valid conceptual setup; score before explaining the repair and do not count this attempt as a pass. Fail: wrong regime/role/sign, invalid incentive logic, replacing utility with monetary sum, treating hypothetical or descriptive data as identified results, or dropping a stated condition that changes the conclusion. For the orientation objective, replacing a printed restriction with an invented rule is a critical error. Unscorable: ambiguous prompt interpretation outside the key, unknown assistance/access/exposure, or unavailable source tuple. No numeric point scale or mastery result is fabricated.

An independent check is fresh only if neither its question nor key has already been exposed, including during earlier diagnostics or feedback. Teach records actual help/access conditions. Correct repetition of an exposed task cannot establish fresh independence. I1 and I2 are reserved for acquisition; D1/D2 are reserved for delayed retrieval.
