sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Symmetric monetary matrix: CC \((a,a)\),CD \((d,c)\),DC \((c,d)\),DD \((b,b)\), with \(c>a>b>d\). A compares first coordinates; B second. Anonymous players cannot communicate in the described setup.
  2. Against C, defect yields \(c>a\); against D, defect yields \(b>d\). D strictly dominates for A and by symmetry B. Therefore DD is the unique Nash equilibrium: either other action still makes D strictly optimal; no probability mixture can reverse a strict comparison. At CC, a player gains \(c-a\) by unilateral D. At DD, switching alone loses \(b-d\).
  3. Mutual cooperation gives each \(a>b\), so both are better than DD. However total in CC is \(2a\), in DD \(2b\) and in a mixed cellc+d. \(c>a>b>d\) alone does not order \(2a\) againstc+d. A claim that CC maximizes every monetary total needs that additional comparison, absent from general source assumptions.
  4. For rational self-regarding players with commonly known finite final period, fixed stage game and additive stage payoffs (possibly positive discounted weights), last-period D is optimal after every history because no future incentive remains. Last-period D is fixed regardless of penultimate choices, so the penultimate current comparison gives D; continue backwards to first. The unique subgame-perfect benchmark defects at every stage after every history, not just on the realized path.
  5. “They will meet again” does not overturn this known-finite logic. The proof does not cover uncertain/indefinite horizon, uncertainty about preferences or changed social preferences. Lecture observed cooperation motivates amendments; it supplies no poll responses or precise rate here.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The prisoner's dilemma: a simultaneous conflict; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The prisoner's dilemma: a simultaneous conflict

In the lecture's prisoner's dilemma, two anonymous players cannot communicate and choose cooperate or defect simultaneously. Simultaneous means each chooses without knowing the other's current action. The first number in each payoff pair belongs to Player A, who chooses the row; the second belongs to Player B, who chooses the column. The monetary units are not specified on the numerical slide. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 29–31

Player A's action B cooperates B defects
Cooperate \((16,16)\) \((8,20)\)
Defect \((20,8)\) \((12,12)\)

The full source slide preserves the numerical matrix and the lecture's dominant-strategy and Nash-equilibrium claims. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 32

Dominance and Nash equilibrium

A strictly dominant strategy gives a player a higher payoff than the alternative for every action of the other player. Agent unpacking of the matrix: if B cooperates, A gets 20 from defecting rather than 16 from cooperating; if B defects, A gets 12 rather than 8. Defection is therefore strictly dominant for A. By symmetry, it is strictly dominant for B too. A Nash equilibrium is a pair of strategies in which neither player benefits from changing their own choice while holding the other's fixed. Because each player's strict best response is always defection, \((D,D)\) is the unique Nash equilibrium under self-regarding preferences. The classroom question on PDF p. 30 has no displayed poll results. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 29–32

Each receives 12 in equilibrium, although mutual cooperation would give each 16. The difference is a conflict between the individually attractive deviation and the jointly preferable cooperative outcome. From \((C,C)\), either player can gain 4 by defecting alone. From \((D,D)\), switching alone to cooperation loses 4. Thus joint improvement does not make unilateral cooperation individually optimal. This illustrates the lecture's argument that privately costly cooperation can increase social welfare while a private incentive points toward defection. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 31–32; payoff interpretation

General payoffs and finite repetition

The lecture's general symmetric matrix has \(c>a>b>d\):

Player A's action B cooperates B defects
Cooperate \((a,a)\) \((d,c)\)
Defect \((c,d)\) \((b,b)\)

Here \(c\) is the payoff from defecting against cooperation, \(a\) the mutual-cooperation payoff, \(b\) the mutual-defection payoff, and \(d\) the payoff from cooperating against defection. The inequalities \(c>a\) and \(b>d\) make defection strictly dominant; \(a>b\) makes mutual cooperation better for both than mutual defection. These inequalities alone do not state that mutual cooperation maximizes the sum among every possible cell, since no condition comparing \(2a\) with \(c+d\) is given. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 33–34; matrix interpretation

The lecture states that the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium of a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma is defection in every period. Agent unpacking of the required benchmark: take a fixed pair of rational, self-regarding players, a commonly known finite final period, the same stage game in every period, and payoffs given by the sum of the stage payoffs, possibly discounted by positive weights. In the last period there is no future reward or punishment left, so both defect after every possible preceding history. In the penultimate period, last-period defection will occur regardless of today's choices, so the current dominant-strategy logic again gives defection. Repeating this argument backward establishes defection at every stage and after every history. This is stronger than just specifying the actions on one realized path. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 34; backward-induction explanation

The result is conditional on that benchmark, especially the known finite horizon and self-regarding preferences. A chance to meet again does not by itself overturn the backward-induction argument. The argument presented here does not cover an uncertain or indefinite horizon, uncertainty about the other player's preferences, or the social-preference changes introduced next. Social Preferences, physical PDF pp. 34–36; scope of the prediction

O006-W1 — Source numerical dilemma

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Use the finished-note matrix with \(a=16, c=20, b=12, d=8\). Agent-created finite-horizon illustration: 3 commonly known periods.

Worked reasoning and result: The symmetric matrix is \(\mathrm{CC}=(16,16)\), \(\mathrm{CD}=(8,20)\), \(\mathrm{DC}=(20,8)\), \(\mathrm{DD}=(12,12)\), satisfying \(c>a>b>d\). A chooses rows and reads first coordinates; B chooses columns and reads second coordinates. Choices are simultaneous, anonymous and without communication. For each player, \(D\) gives \(20>16\) against \(C\) and \(12>8\) against \(D\). \(D\) strictly dominates; \((D,D)\) is the unique monetary Nash equilibrium, stable against unilateral changes. Defecting alone from \(\mathrm{CC}\) gains \(4\); switching alone from \(\mathrm{DD}\) to \(C\) loses \(4\). \(\mathrm{CC}\) gives each \(16>12\) compared with \(\mathrm{DD}\). Cell totals are \(\mathrm{CC}=32\), \(\mathrm{DD}=24\), \(\text{mixed}=28\); \(\mathrm{CC}\) has the largest total in this example. The general ordering alone does not compare \(2a\) with \(c+d\). That future defection is fixed regardless of the previous action, making \(D\) optimal in period \(2\); repeat backwards to period \(1\). The cooperation premium compensates a private cost. The cost can differ depending on B’s action, so a premium between the two costs does not identify A’s action without its beliefs. Delta is in money-equivalent utility units and \(\pi\) is a probability in \([0,1]\); B remains self-regarding. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Start from \(\mathrm{CC}:(a,a)\), \(\mathrm{CD}:(d,c)\), \(\mathrm{DC}:(c,d)\), \(\mathrm{DD}:(b,b)\), with \(c>a>b>d\). Add \(\delta\) only when A chooses \(C\): \(\mathrm{CC}\) utility \((a+\delta ,a)\), \(\mathrm{CD}:(d+\delta,c)\); the other row remains \((c,d),(b,b)\). Money itself has not increased by \(\delta\).
  2. Against \(B=C\), compare \(a+\delta\) with \(c\): A strictly cooperates iff \(\delta >c-a\). Against \(B=D\) compare \(d+\delta\) with \(b\): cooperation iff \(\delta >b-d\). Equality is indifference in the corresponding comparison.
  3. Below both thresholds, \(D\) is strictly dominant (the lecture’s “egoist” behavior label, even if a small positive premium exists). Above both, \(C\) is strictly dominant (“dominant-strategy altruist”). Intermediate premiums are called “best-response altruists”, with two possible orderings: \(c-a<\delta <b-d\) yields \(C\) against \(C\) and \(D\) against \(D\); \(b-d<\delta <c-a\) yields \(D\) against \(C\) and \(C\) against \(D\). \(c>a>b>d\) alone cannot select an ordering.
  4. At a simultaneous choice A does not observe B’s current action. With \(\pi=\Pr(B=C)\), expected \(C\) utility is \(\pi(a+\delta)+(1-\pi)(d+\delta)\), expected \(D\) utility is \(\pi c+(1-\pi)b\). Subtract: \(\Delta U=\delta-[\pi(c-a)+(1-\pi)(b-d)]\). Choose \(C\) if positive, \(D\) if negative, tie if zero. This is the finished notes’ algebraic derivation, not an estimated belief model.
  5. B’s own monetary payoffs are unchanged; \(c>a\) and \(b>d\) keep \(D\) strictly dominant for B. Correctly anticipating a selfish B means \(\pi =0\), so compare \(\delta\) to \(b-d\). In the first intermediate ordering A then defects; in the second it cooperates. Therefore the lecture’s broad claim that any intermediate type guarantees observed cooperation requires qualification.
  6. In the original \(a=16,c=20,b=12,d=8\) matrix both costs are \(4\): \(\delta <4\) gives \(D\), \(\delta >4\) gives \(C\), \(\delta =4\) ties against either B action. No nonempty intermediate interval exists. A’s \(C\) at \(\delta >4\) is paired with B’s \(D\), not mutual cooperation.
  7. The separate reciprocity explanation requires a belief about kindness in a simultaneous game; a trustee instead observes the prior transfer in sequential trust. The notes supply no quantitative reciprocity threshold, full study methods or numerical cooperation rate. Social preferences can increase welfare, conditional on incentives, preferences and beliefs, rather than always doing so.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage A warm-glow premium can change best responses; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

A warm-glow premium can change best responses

The lecture observes that many subjects cooperate to some extent even in finitely repeated or one-shot versions. It proposes altruism or efficiency-seeking as one explanation, represented by a warm-glow premium \(\delta\) for Player 1's act of cooperating. The premium is measured in money-equivalent utility units and is added to Player 1's payoff whenever Player 1 cooperates, regardless of Player 2's action. Player 2 remains selfish. In this illustration Player 1 is A, the row player. This particular additive model captures a benefit from the act of cooperation; it is not the same formula as directly weighting the other person's payoff in the social-preference model. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35

Full source slide: only A's cooperative-row payoffs acquire \(\delta\). The source's classification and its final cooperation assertion remain visible; the assertion is qualified below. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35

Deriving the two thresholds

Agent unpacking of the lecture's altered matrix: when B cooperates, A compares \(a+\delta\) with \(c\). Cooperation is strictly preferred when

\[a+\delta>c \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \delta>c-a.\]

When B defects, A compares \(d+\delta\) with \(b\), giving

\[d+\delta>b \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \delta>b-d.\]

The two positive thresholds are the monetary costs of choosing cooperation in the two situations. If \(\delta<\min(c-a,b-d)\), neither cost is compensated and A strictly prefers defection against either action. The lecture labels this player an egoist in its behavioral classification, even though a small positive premium may be present. If \(\delta>\max(c-a,b-d)\), both costs are compensated and cooperation is strictly dominant: the lecture calls this a dominant-strategy altruist. At equality with either threshold, A is indifferent in the corresponding comparison, so the strict classifications do not apply there. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35; threshold derivation

For intermediate values, the lecture uses the name best-response altruist. There are two distinct orderings, and \(c>a>b>d\) alone does not choose between them:

Ordering and intermediate premium A's best response if B cooperates A's best response if B defects
\(c-a<\delta<b-d\) Cooperate Defect
\(b-d<\delta<c-a\) Defect Cooperate

In the first case cooperation is conditional on B's cooperation; in the second, the premium covers the cost of cooperating against defection but not the cost of cooperating against cooperation. Agent derivation with beliefs: if A assigns probability \(\pi\) to B cooperating, its expected utility advantage of cooperation is

\[\begin{aligned} \Delta U_A &=\pi(a+\delta)+(1-\pi)(d+\delta) -\bigl[\pi c+(1-\pi)b\bigr]\\ &=\delta-\bigl[\pi(c-a)+(1-\pi)(b-d)\bigr]. \end{aligned}\]

A strictly cooperates if this expression is positive, defects if it is negative, and is indifferent at zero. Thus an intermediate premium generally requires beliefs about B's action to predict A's choice. This calculation unpacks the displayed matrix; the lecture does not supply this expected-utility equation. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35; agent derivation

The numerical threshold and a source qualification

In the numerical game, \(c-a=20-16=4\) and \(b-d=12-8=4\). Therefore \(\delta<4\) makes defection strictly dominant for A, while \(\delta>4\) makes cooperation strictly dominant. At \(\delta=4\), A is indifferent between the actions against either choice of B. There is no nonempty intermediate interval in this particular matrix because the two thresholds coincide. Since B remains selfish and its own payoffs are unchanged, B continues to defect. Consequently a premium greater than 4 predicts A cooperating against B's defection, rather than mutual cooperation. These are agent calculations from the source's numerical and altered matrices. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 32 Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35

Source assertion and limitation: PDF p. 35 says that cooperation will be observed whenever players include dominant-strategy altruists or best-response altruists. The claim is broader than the displayed matrix supports without qualifications. A dominant-strategy altruist does cooperate. But a best-response altruist with \(c-a<\delta<b-d\), correctly expecting the stipulated selfish B to defect, also defects. Conversely, a best-response altruist with \(b-d<\delta<c-a\) cooperates against B's defection. The source statement is retained here as a statement from the lecture; the payoff ordering and beliefs must be specified before extending it to every player in the intermediate category. Merely having that category in a population does not guarantee observed cooperation or mutual cooperation. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 35, final bullet

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Reciprocity needs an expectation about the other player; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Reciprocity needs an expectation about the other player

The lecture's second explanation is positive reciprocity combined with the belief that the other person will cooperate. It cites Dawes and Thaler (1988) beside the observation that cooperation occurs even with a finite number of interactions, sometimes only once; the uploaded slide does not supply the underlying study design, sample, or numerical cooperation rate. Positive reciprocity means wanting to respond kindly to perceived kindness. In a simultaneous game there is no observed current action to reciprocate at the moment of choice, so an expectation about the other's cooperation is part of this proposed explanation. The lecture does not specify a separate payoff formula or a quantitative belief threshold for this mechanism. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 36

This differs from the trust game, where the trustee observes the initial transfer before returning money. It also differs from the unconditional warm-glow premium: a desire to reward kindness depends on how the other player's behavior is perceived or expected. The reciprocity model makes this dependence explicit. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 22 Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 36; connection between games

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What these games establish; fingerprint e14303da01e107f5fec8496b95506702aef07ede33359781307e6befec155659. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What these games establish

The trust game separates surplus creation from its subsequent division; the prisoner's dilemma exposes a dominant individual incentive that conflicts with mutual gains. Their no-trust or defection benchmarks follow from specified self-regarding preferences and expectations, not from the game labels alone. The lecture's empirical descriptions motivate broader preferences, and its warm-glow matrix shows exactly how a sufficiently large nonmonetary benefit can change a best response. Intermediate benefits and reciprocity require attention to the other player's expected behavior. The lecture's final lesson is that many motivations extend beyond pure selfishness and that social preferences can increase social welfare, a possibility whose realization depends on the game, preferences, and beliefs. Social Preferences, physical PDF p. 37

O007-W1 — Two threshold orders

Item version: v1. Role: worked instruction.

Setup: Agent-created hypothetical pair: game F has \((a,c,b,d)=(6,7,4,0), \delta =2\); game G has \((6,10,4,3), \delta =2\). Compute altered matrices, best responses and \(\pi =0,1/2,1\) choices, including a tie probability; compare the original source matrix and reciprocity limits.

Worked reasoning and result: For \((a,c,b,d)=(6,7,4,0)\), \(\delta=2\), the altered utility matrix is \(\mathrm{CC}=(8,6)\), \(\mathrm{CD}=(2,7)\), \(\mathrm{DC}=(7,0)\), \(\mathrm{DD}=(4,4)\); only A’s cooperative row receives the utility premium. Thresholds are \(c-a=1, b-d=4\). Best response to \(C\) is \(C\) and to \(D\) is \(D\); this is the \(c-a<\delta <b-d\) ordering. For \(\delta <1\), \(D\) is strictly dominant; for \(\delta >4\), \(C\) is strictly dominant. At \(\delta =1\), A ties against \(C\); at \(\delta =4\), A ties against \(D\), with the other comparison determined separately. Expected advantage is \(\delta-[\pi(c-a)+(1-\pi)(b-d)]\). At \(\pi =0,1/2,1\) its values are \(-2\), \(-0.5\), \(1\), giving \(D\), \(D\), \(C\). The tie probability is \(0.666667\) (exactly \((4-2)/(4-1)\)); both actions give equal expected utility there. B compares unchanged \(c>a\) and \(b>d\), so strictly defects against either A action. Correctly anticipating B sets \(\pi =0\) and gives \((D,D)\). The premium is not additional monetary output.

For \((a,c,b,d)=(6,10,4,3)\), \(\delta=2\), the altered utility matrix is \(\mathrm{CC}=(8,6)\), \(\mathrm{CD}=(5,10)\), \(\mathrm{DC}=(10,3)\), \(\mathrm{DD}=(4,4)\); only A’s cooperative row receives the utility premium. Thresholds are \(c-a=4, b-d=1\). Best response to \(C\) is \(D\) and to \(D\) is \(C\); this is the \(b-d<\delta <c-a\) ordering. For \(\delta <1\), \(D\) is strictly dominant; for \(\delta >4\), \(C\) is strictly dominant. At \(\delta =4\), A ties against \(C\); at \(\delta =1\), A ties against \(D\), with the other comparison determined separately. Expected advantage is \(\delta-[\pi(c-a)+(1-\pi)(b-d)]\). At \(\pi =0,1/2,1\) its values are \(1\), \(-0.5\), \(-2\), giving \(C\), \(D\), \(D\). The tie probability is \(0.333333\) (exactly \((1-2)/(1-4)\)); both actions give equal expected utility there. B compares unchanged \(c>a\) and \(b>d\), so strictly defects against either A action. Correctly anticipating B sets \(\pi =0\) and gives \((C,D)\). The premium is not additional monetary output.

In the original source game \(a=16,c=20,b=12,d=8\), both costs are 4. Delta below 4 makes A defect, above 4 makes A cooperate, at 4 A ties against either action; there is no nonempty intermediate interval. B remains selfish and defects, so a large premium predicts (C,D), not mutual cooperation. The source’s broad cooperation claim holds for dominant-strategy altruists; an intermediate type cooperates or defects depending on threshold order and beliefs. Warm glow is an unconditional utility benefit from A’s act, distinct from directly weighting B’s payoff. Positive reciprocity depends on perceived/expected kindness; simultaneous choices require a belief, whereas a trustee observes the prior transfer. No separate quantitative reciprocity formula/belief threshold, full study methods or cooperation rate is supplied. Social preferences can raise welfare conditionally; spite, incentives and beliefs prevent a universal claim.

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks
  • R1: Reconstruct supplied course identity, teaching/preparation/prerequisite and appointment information with its documentary scope.
  • R2: Apply exam format, scoring, tool restrictions and integrity declaration accurately.
  • R3: Distinguish four offered slots from three attempts; retrieve dates/times/room, booking limits, printed grade bands and absent rounding rule.
  • R4: Separate completed expanded Week 1 learning from later syllabus/sample exam orientation, absent answer keys/polls and conditional misperceptions; avoid claiming a personal deadline or full exam readiness.

Every I1, I2, D1, D2 and C1 question/key explicitly addresses all required components above. The sole acquisition route is two separate, distinct, fresh unassisted passes on I1 and I2 under the current criterion and compatible tuple. Worked/support/diagnostic/correction items and delayed items are not acquisition substitutes. No shorter question silently fills a missing component. The fixed practice inputs differ across W1/S1/I1/I2/D1/D2/C1; learning constants from the notes remain common where retrieval of those exact facts is the outcome.

Pass: all essential components, necessary reasoning, assumptions and interpretation limits are present, with accurate outputs. Accept equivalent wording, correct alternative algebra and exact fractions or consistent rounding that preserves inequalities/ties. Partial: a missing component or isolated arithmetic/transcription slip with valid conceptual setup; score before explaining the repair and do not count this attempt as a pass. Fail: wrong regime/role/sign, invalid incentive logic, replacing utility with monetary sum, treating hypothetical or descriptive data as identified results, or dropping a stated condition that changes the conclusion. For the orientation objective, replacing a printed restriction with an invented rule is a critical error. Unscorable: ambiguous prompt interpretation outside the key, unknown assistance/access/exposure, or unavailable source tuple. No numeric point scale or mastery result is fabricated.

An independent check is fresh only if neither its question nor key has already been exposed, including during earlier diagnostics or feedback. Teach records actual help/access conditions. Correct repetition of an exposed task cannot establish fresh independence. I1 and I2 are reserved for acquisition; D1/D2 are reserved for delayed retrieval.

sections.html:
Check the prerequisites
  • O003 outcome and repair route: payoff branches and equality boundaries determine a social utility term’s interpretation.
  • O004 outcome and repair route: reciprocal treatment differs from a payoff-only concern and can alter marginal willingness to help.

O009-P1, item_version 1, prerequisite_diagnostic. Prompt: In a piecewise other-regarding utility, why must the correct payoff ordering be chosen? Does reciprocity depend only on the final payoff pair, and does adding a constant to utility change its maximizer?

Complete key and rubric: The payoff ordering selects the correct weight/branch. Reciprocity can depend on prior treatment or intentions as O004 distinguishes from payoff-only motives. Adding the same constant at every effort changes utility levels but not rankings/marginal effort incentives. Require all clauses; repair O003 branches and O004 treatment distinction. Pass requires every requested reason and result; partial for an omitted reason or unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This diagnostic never counts as acquisition. Current or explicitly compatible committed independent prerequisite evidence may permit skipping its check; familiarity alone cannot. Use the cited complete prerequisite lesson or the named included foundation, then the worked example, after a partial/failing entry check.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Effort, contracts and social motivations; fingerprint 9b7365693d9f801e0a0ff180c3fd9801b7ad8976661455d7d8299756e0090ede. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Effort, contracts and social motivations

Why might a fixed wage change effort even when it does not change the monetary reward for an extra unit of work? The lecture first derives the self-regarding incentive benchmark, then changes the worker's utility. This separates an incentive effect from a social response to the employer or co-workers. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 4–9

The map follows the lecture's model and its transition to field evidence. The core reasoning is marginal: a benefit that changes the level of utility but not its slope with respect to effort need not change effort. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 5–9

The self-regarding principal-agent benchmark

The principal employs an agent whose effort \(e\) is not directly observable. Output is \(f(e)+\varepsilon\), with \(f'(e)>0\), \(f''(e)<0\) and mean-zero noise. Effort costs \(d(e)\), where \(d'(e)>0\) and \(d''(e)>0\). More effort raises expected output at a decreasing rate while its marginal cost rises. The simplified expected-pay contract is

\[y(e)=w+b f(e),\]

where \(w\) is fixed pay and \(b\) is the worker's output share. In the risk-neutral expected-pay representation, the noise has zero expected monetary contribution. If the actual contract pays on noisy observed output, a risk-averse worker would need a separate treatment of risk; that is outside the displayed benchmark. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 5–6

The selfish worker chooses

\[e^*(w,b)\in\arg\max_e\{w+b f(e)-d(e)\}.\]

At an interior differentiable optimum,

\[b f'(e^*)=d'(e^*).\]

An extra unit of effort produces \(f'(e)\) expected output, of which the worker receives \(b f'(e)\); the worker compares that reward with \(d'(e)\). Fixed pay \(w\) vanishes from this derivative. Under the stated concavity/convexity conditions the utility is concave for a nonnegative output share. If effort must be nonnegative, a corner is possible: for \(b=0\), utility falls with effort and the optimum is the lowest feasible effort, written \(e=0\) in the lecture. The equality condition does not apply at that corner. A higher fixed wage raises the level of selfish utility but supplies no extra marginal monetary reward for effort in this particular model. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 5–6

The principal anticipates the agent's choice and writes

\[\max_{w,b}\{(1-b)f(e^*(w,b))-w\}.\]

This is expected output retained by the principal less fixed pay. The displayed objective does not supply participation constraints, outside options, permissible wages or a full risk-sharing problem, so it should not be used to solve an unrestricted global optimum for \(w\). Its role here is to show why the principal cares about the agent's effort response. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 6

Adding a marginal social motive

The lecture adds a social component,

\[U_i=w+b f(e_i)-d(e_i)+S(e_i),\]

giving the interior condition

\[b f'(e_i)+\frac{\partial S}{\partial e_i}=d'(e_i).\]

The new term measures the utility benefit or cost of how extra effort affects socially valued outcomes. If it is positive, effort can be worthwhile even with little direct marginal pay. This is a conditional model mechanism, not a claim that every gift raises effort. For a fixed wage to change the optimum, it must change a relevant marginal social motive, such as perceived kindness toward the employer, rather than simply add a constant to \(S\). L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7

For altruism, the slide writes \(S_i=\sigma_{ij}U_j(e_i)\) with a positive weight on the other person's utility. If the employer benefits from extra effort, then \(\partial S_i/\partial e_i=\sigma_{ij}U_j'(e_i)\) can be positive. If extra effort instead harms a cared-for peer, the same positive concern produces a negative social derivative and can lower effort. For reciprocity, kind treatment can make helping the employer attractive, while unkind treatment can reduce that willingness or create a motive to harm. This depends on the treatment and its perceived intentions, not only on final wage levels. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7, 9

For inequality aversion, the source gives the schematic \(S_i=\sigma_{ij}|y_i-y_j|\) with \(\sigma_{ij}<0\). A payoff gap lowers utility, but the effect on effort depends on how effort changes the two payoffs. The slide's intuition is that a worker with an outcome above the norm may reduce effort, while one below it may increase effort. When own payoff rises with effort and peer payoff is fixed, the absolute gap rises with effort above the peer, so the negative coefficient creates a negative social derivative; below the peer the gap falls with effort, giving a positive social derivative. More generally, the sign depends on how effort changes the payoff gap. That intuition requires a channel from effort into payoffs or socially interpreted contributions. If both own and peer monetary wages are literally fixed and independent of effort, the displayed absolute wage gap is constant: this term alone has zero effort derivative and cannot generate that response. The comparison is also nondifferentiable at equal pay. Treat the formula as a simplified motivation, not a general proof of every relative-pay effect. The Week 1 note gives the fuller payoff-weight distinctions. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7 Models of Social Preferences

Wage rigidity and the gift-exchange hypothesis

The opening supply-demand picture draws a wage above the market-clearing intersection, so labour supplied exceeds labour demanded. The horizontal gap is unemployment in that illustration. It motivates the question of why firms might sustain wages above a competitive benchmark; the drawing does not establish the cause of observed unemployment. Akerlof's gift-exchange idea is that firms offer favourable wages and workers reciprocate with effort above the minimum. Such responses can make high wages privately worthwhile under some conditions. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 2–3, 9

Read the wage, employment and excess-supply gap together. The later field studies test particular wage/effort responses, rather than proving a complete macroeconomic explanation from this stylized graph. The Sli.do prompt on the preceding lecture pages records a question, not observed class poll results. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 2–4

The principal-agent derivation and the distinction between marginal incentives and social motives are core because they generate predictions. The field applications then ask whether those predictions survive real effort, time and context. No slide or these notes establish that any specific derivation will appear in an exam. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 4–9, 35

O009-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Use a hypothetical risk-neutral expected-pay model on \(0\leq e\leq 9\): \(f(e)=10e-e^2/2\), \(d(e)=2e+e^2/2\), contract \(y=w+b f(e)\) with \(w=10\) and \(b=0.5\). Derive the selfish marginal condition and optimum, checking concavity and corners. Does increasing only \(w\) by 5 change effort? Compare a fixed-pay contract \(b=0\) without social utility. Now add the explicitly supplied \(S(e)=3e\) and solve effort. Explain how altruistic concern can increase or reduce the social derivative, why a literally fixed own/peer wage gap alone cannot affect effort, and what is unresolved at equality. State the principal’s expected objective and why an unrestricted optimum for its wage cannot be solved from these notes alone.

Complete solution and essential rubric: \(f^{\prime}(e)=10-e>0\) on the supplied domain and \(f^{\prime\prime}=-1\); \(d^{\prime}(e)=2+e>0\) and \(d^{\prime\prime}=1\). Selfish derivative is \(b(10-e)-(2+e)\), second derivative \(-(b+1)<0\), and the unconstrained solution is \((0.5(10)-2)/(0.5+1)=2.00000000\) here, inside the bounds. Clipping/checking endpoints handles a corner. Fixed \(w\) disappears from the derivative, so a 5-unit wage increase does not change effort in this benchmark. At \(b=0\) and no social term the objective decreases with effort, giving the lowest feasible effort 0. With \(S^{\prime}(e)=3\), solve \(b(10-e)+3=2+e\), yielding \(4.00000000\), again feasible. Positive altruistic weight times the other person’s effort-induced utility derivative can be positive when helping them or negative when effort harms them; reciprocity depends on treatment/intentions. A negative coefficient on \(|y_i-y_j|\) has zero effort derivative if both payoffs are literally effort-independent. With an effort-varying gap its derivative may differ above/below the peer; the absolute value is nondifferentiable at equality. The principal anticipates effort and maximizes \((1-b)f(e^*(w,b))-w\), but participation/outside-option/feasible-wage/risk-sharing constraints are absent, so no unrestricted global wage optimum or complete macro-unemployment explanation is inferred. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Gift exchange in labour-market field experiments; fingerprint 9302e6c35313a9e16a1e62736c03c3e078afc09b76cc2ea12d7ff16331d489dd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Gift exchange in labour-market field experiments

Does a wage gift buy sustained additional effort, and does the form of a gift matter? These experiments hold important features of employment fixed while varying pay or presentation. Their comparisons test the social-motivation hypothesis against the fixed-pay selfish benchmark, but the duration and implementation of each treatment remain part of the conclusion. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 9–24

The map organizes the supplied studies around the treatment, time profile and interpretation. A positive early response, a lasting response and a profitable response are three different claims. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 10–24

Gneezy and List: the response can fade

In the library task, workers were recruited for six hours of entering book records at $12 per hour. The gift group unexpectedly received $20 per hour. Effort was measured as books entered in successive 90-minute intervals, not a hypothetical effort number. The lecture's figure shows a higher first-block output in the gift condition, followed by convergence. Approximate plotted means are about 52 versus 41 books initially and about 40 in each condition in the final interval. Do not read those graphical approximations as individually observed outcomes. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 10–12

In the fundraising task, the announced wage was $10 per hour; after training the gift group was told it would receive $20. The source describes two days of fundraising work and displays the comparison for three-hour blocks before and after lunch. The vertical axis is money raised for the organization, rather than the solicitor's own wage. Before lunch the gift group collected about $11 per hour versus $6.4–6.5 in the control; after lunch the amounts were much closer. A common time trend alone would not explain why the treatment difference shrinks: the relevant comparison is the difference between groups in each period. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 13–14

The lecture discusses an initially emotional response and subsequent adaptation of the wage reference point as possible explanations. The time pattern itself does not uniquely distinguish those psychological mechanisms. The authors conclude that the wage gifts did not maximize employer returns in these settings: the output gain was too limited relative to the higher wage bill. This does not imply that reciprocity never exists or that every employer should pay the lowest feasible wage. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 15

Primary-source check: Gneezy and List (2006), Econometrica 74(5), 1365–1384, author PDF §§2–3, physical pp. 3–8, verifies the announced/surprise wages, six-hour library task, measured outcomes and fading difference. Its detailed book means are 51.7/44.9/41.7/40.3 for gift and 40.7/40.5/41.2/39.6 for control. The brief one-time employment design was chosen partly to limit future-employment incentives. This is a bounded verification of the lecture examples, not ingestion of the full paper. Consulted author PDF.

Kube, Maréchal and Puppe: positive and negative responses differ

The lecture's 2006 working-paper example recruits workers for a six-hour book-record task at €15 per hour. The control receives €15, a kind treatment €20 and an unkind treatment €10. The lower wage is a wage cut, not a dismissal or a cut in the number of workers. The figure plots average books entered over time. The wage-cut group remains well below control throughout the task; the wage-gift group's advantage is smaller and less decisive. A negative wage surprise can therefore have a more persistent effect than an equivalent positive surprise in this setting. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 16–18

The intended comparison is kind/control/unkind treatment with effort otherwise measured in the same units. “The effects are asymmetric” does not mean their magnitudes must be equal with opposite signs, nor does the graph identify a universal wage-cut elasticity. The source's Sli.do prediction prompt supplies no class response data. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 17–18

The currency of reciprocity: money and a thermos bottle

The lecture next uses Kube, Maréchal and Puppe (2011). Workers enter library records at a fixed wage of \(\text{€}12\) per hour. A surprise monetary gift of \(\text{€}7\) costs roughly \(20\%\) of baseline task pay (\(\frac{\text{€}12}{\text{hour}}\times3\text{ hours}=\text{€}36\), so \(\text{€}7/\text{€}36\approx19.4\%\); post-gift pay is \(\text{€}43\)); the alternative is a thermos bottle worth \(\text{€}7\). There is no prospect of repeat employment, and output quantity and quality are tracked. Equal employer expenditure permits a comparison of the form of the gift, rather than a simple comparison of a large and a small gift. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 19–20

The cash treatment gives only a small, statistically undetected gain relative to baseline; the bottle treatment has a much larger gain. The graph measures characters entered per 30-minute interval. In the primary 2011 manuscript, the reported average bottle gain is about 25%. A price-tag treatment tells recipients the bottle's €7 value and still produces substantial effort, weakening the explanation that the effect arises solely because workers overestimate the price. This control does not remove every possible difference in perceived kindness, attention or beliefs. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 20–21

Perhaps workers simply like the bottle more? In the choice treatment, around 80% choose cash rather than the bottle, yet work effort remains comparable to the bottle condition. Preference for receiving money and effort in response to a considerate offer are different outcomes. This undermines a simple story that the bottle works only because recipients value its consumption more than €7. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 22

The origami treatment folds a €5 note into a shirt and adds a €2 coin with a smiley. The worker still receives €7, but presentation visibly takes time and care. The source reports approximately 30% higher effort than baseline. Together with the choice and price-tag controls, this supports the importance of the gift's social meaning and perceived thoughtfulness. It does not uniquely identify a complete psychological mechanism or establish that elaborate gifts always outperform cash. Physical p. 24 repeats the origami photograph/presentation while stating the lesson; both presentations are accounted for by the same explanation. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 23–24

Version check: the consulted KIT 2011 working paper, title page and methods/results on printed pp. 5–18, contains the choice and origami treatments and the roughly 25%/30% results. The same title also circulated in a January 2010 author PDF, with different treatments/results; its 92.4% cash-choice figure and 30% bottle estimate should not replace the lecture's 2011 comparison. The published article is American Economic Review 102(4), 1644–1662 (2012); the lecture's 2011 date refers to its working-paper version.

What the comparisons establish

The fixed-pay model supplies a benchmark of no marginal monetary reason to work harder. Unexpected treatment changes can nevertheless alter real effort. The empirical questions then become which treatment, for how long, with what cost, and under what interpretation. The studies are core applications because their controls help separate a marginal incentive from reciprocity, relative valuation and presentation; they do not allow a single universal estimate of gift exchange. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 15, 18–24, 35

Incremental revenue is \(16(0.5)=8.00000000\); added wage bill is \(6(2)=12.00000000\), so hypothetical incremental net return is \(-4.00000000\). The effect fades in this supplied profile; initial, persistent and profitable responses are separate claims. These invented calculations are not a re-estimate of the studies. Attention, perceived kindness, beliefs and reference adaptation remain overlapping explanations; no universal gift elasticity or complete unemployment cause is proved. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, Relative pay and charitable gift exchange, fingerprint f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Relative pay and charitable gift exchange

Social preferences can make the treatment of co-workers or donors relevant even when own monetary pay is fixed. The lecture combines a workplace comparison experiment with a fundraising experiment. Their common logic is to vary a socially meaningful feature while keeping a useful monetary benchmark clear. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 25–35

This map places the comparison group and outcome denominator before the substantive conclusion. It follows the two supplied applications and prevents treating attendance, donation frequency and donation amounts as interchangeable. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26–34

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Relative wages with own wage held fixed; fingerprint f25609e10a80282755875d6639b5d4cc8b32423bdac3240e176c3a7e277e95ef. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Relative wages with own wage held fixed

Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani's Indian field experiment organizes workers into teams whose members make the same product in proximity, while production remains individual. Teams are assigned either a flat common daily wage or different wages linked to baseline productivity rank. Comparisons across treatments can hold a worker's own absolute wage fixed while changing what co-workers receive. Without this comparison, a low-paid worker's lower effort could simply reflect lower own pay rather than relative-pay concerns. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26

The lecture reports that workers paid less than peers reduce output by 12% and are 13% less likely to come to work, while higher relative pay produces no detected effort increase. These are the lecture's reported percentages, not an instruction to relabel the attendance change as 13 percentage points. Nor does “no detected increase” prove an exactly zero effect for every worker. The Sli.do page asks for a prediction but shows no poll results. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 27–28

Perceived justification matters: when the pay gap is clearly supported by observed baseline productivity differences, the negative effect is not detected. The simple fact of unequal pay therefore does not fully determine the response; information about why pay differs changes the interpretation. The source concludes that inequality was bad for the firm in the studied comparison. Treat that as an application-specific result, not a general theorem that every wage difference reduces output. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 28

The lesson links to inequality aversion and fairness perceptions, but the design does not identify one utility function merely from a negative response. A preference for equality, resentment about unjustified treatment and beliefs about management can generate overlapping predictions. The model note also explains why a utility penalty on an entirely effort-independent fixed wage gap cannot mechanically derive every effort effect without an additional channel. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7, 26–28 Adding a marginal social motive
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
O011-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: A hypothetical unequal-pay workplace comparison holds a low-paid worker’s own daily wage fixed across equal-pay and peer-higher-pay teams, with the same individual production task. Baseline output is 100 units; the unequal-pay condition reduces it by 12%. Baseline attendance probability is 0.8; for this hypothetical calculation “13.0% less likely” explicitly means a relative reduction from that baseline. Calculate output, attendance probability and percentage-point change. Explain the identifying comparison, how “the pay gap is visibly explained by prior productivity” would bear on the interpretation, and what the lecture’s actual 12%/13% reports do and do not establish. Does the design identify a unique inequality-aversion utility, or can a constant fixed wage-gap penalty by itself derive effort?

Complete solution and essential rubric: Output becomes \(100(1-.12)=88.00000000\) units. Under the expressly supplied relative-probability convention, attendance becomes \(0.8(1-0.13)=0.69600000\), a change of \(-10.40000000\) percentage points. Relative percent and percentage points differ; the lecture’s actual 13% statement cannot be converted to 13 points or a numerical probability without a baseline and precise definition. Keeping own wage fixed while changing peers’ wages separates relative-pay treatment from an own-wage-level explanation, subject to the randomized design and measured task. Clear baseline-productivity justification can change perceived fairness; the lecture reports no detected negative effect under visible justification, not a theorem that any wage gap is harmless. Its 12% output/13% attendance reports are source-reported setting-specific effects and “no detected” high-pay increase is not proof of exact zero. Equality concerns, resentment, fairness beliefs and management intentions can overlap. A literally fixed gap term is constant in effort and has zero derivative; a further effort/payoff or social-meaning channel is needed. No unique utility function or universal employment effect is identified. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

interactions.prompt_html:
O011-I1

O011-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A hypothetical unequal-pay workplace comparison holds a low-paid worker’s own daily wage fixed across equal-pay and peer-higher-pay teams, with the same individual production task. Baseline output is 120 units; the unequal-pay condition reduces it by 12%. Baseline attendance probability is 0.75; for this hypothetical calculation “13.0% less likely” explicitly means a relative reduction from that baseline. Calculate output, attendance probability and percentage-point change. Explain the identifying comparison, how “workers observe a clear performance basis for unequal pay” would bear on the interpretation, and what the lecture’s actual 12%/13% reports do and do not establish. Does the design identify a unique inequality-aversion utility, or can a constant fixed wage-gap penalty by itself derive effort?
interactions.solution_html:
Complete solution and essential rubric: Output becomes \(120(1-.12)=105.60000000\) units. Under the expressly supplied relative-probability convention, attendance becomes \(0.75(1-0.13)=0.65250000\), a change of \(-9.75000000\) percentage points. Relative percent and percentage points differ; the lecture’s actual 13% statement cannot be converted to 13 points or a numerical probability without a baseline and precise definition. Keeping own wage fixed while changing peers’ wages separates relative-pay treatment from an own-wage-level explanation, subject to the randomized design and measured task. Clear baseline-productivity justification can change perceived fairness; the lecture reports no detected negative effect under visible justification, not a theorem that any wage gap is harmless. Its 12% output/13% attendance reports are source-reported setting-specific effects and “no detected” high-pay increase is not proof of exact zero. Equality concerns, resentment, fairness beliefs and management intentions can overlap. A literally fixed gap term is constant in effort and has zero derivative; a further effort/payoff or social-meaning channel is needed. No unique utility function or universal employment effect is identified. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

I1/I2 are immediate checks; D1/D2 are distinct parallel variants reserved where possible for delayed checks. A delayed success requires an unused form before recap, no help/solution access, and at least 24 actual elapsed hours after acquisition and the most recent relevant teaching/solution exposure. Record intervening exposure. A calendar-date change alone is insufficient; an early D attempt is immediate evidence only.

sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

Social preferences can make the treatment of co-workers or donors relevant even when own monetary pay is fixed. The lecture combines a workplace comparison experiment with a fundraising experiment. Their common logic is to vary a socially meaningful feature while keeping a useful monetary benchmark clear. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 25–35

This map places the comparison group and outcome denominator before the substantive conclusion. It follows the two supplied applications and prevents treating attendance, donation frequency and donation amounts as interchangeable. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26–34

Relative wages with own wage held fixed

Breza, Kaur and Shamdasani's Indian field experiment organizes workers into teams whose members make the same product in proximity, while production remains individual. Teams are assigned either a flat common daily wage or different wages linked to baseline productivity rank. Comparisons across treatments can hold a worker's own absolute wage fixed while changing what co-workers receive. Without this comparison, a low-paid worker's lower effort could simply reflect lower own pay rather than relative-pay concerns. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 26

The lecture reports that workers paid less than peers reduce output by 12% and are 13% less likely to come to work, while higher relative pay produces no detected effort increase. These are the lecture's reported percentages, not an instruction to relabel the attendance change as 13 percentage points. Nor does “no detected increase” prove an exactly zero effect for every worker. The Sli.do page asks for a prediction but shows no poll results. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 27–28

Perceived justification matters: when the pay gap is clearly supported by observed baseline productivity differences, the negative effect is not detected. The simple fact of unequal pay therefore does not fully determine the response; information about why pay differs changes the interpretation. The source concludes that inequality was bad for the firm in the studied comparison. Treat that as an application-specific result, not a general theorem that every wage difference reduces output. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 28

The lesson links to inequality aversion and fairness perceptions, but the design does not identify one utility function merely from a negative response. A preference for equality, resentment about unjustified treatment and beliefs about management can generate overlapping predictions. The model note also explains why a utility penalty on an entirely effort-independent fixed wage gap cannot mechanically derive every effort effect without an additional channel. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 7, 26–28 Adding a marginal social motive

Falk: a gift before the donation decision

Falk's 2007 field experiment sends roughly 10,000 letters for an education charity supporting schools in Bangladesh, addressed to potential donors in Switzerland. The randomized treatments contain no gift, one postcard, or four postcards. The postcards are illustrated with a child's drawing; the drawing is part of the gift treatment, not evidence about an individual donor's circumstances. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 29–31

The theory comparison assumes that the solicitation and recipient's information are otherwise comparable. Pure selfishness without another benefit predicts no donation. Simple altruism about the charity's work alone need not respond to gift size if relevant information and beliefs remain fixed. Reciprocity predicts a stronger response to a larger kind gesture. These predictions depend on the maintained assumptions: gifts might also affect attention, beliefs, warm glow or perceived solicitation costs, so a response gradient is consistent with reciprocity rather than a unique proof of it. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 30

Treatment Letters Donations Rounded donation frequency
No gift 3,262 397 0.12
Small gift 3,237 465 0.14
Large gift 3,347 691 0.21

These source counts sum to 9,846 letters, explaining why “roughly 10,000” is an approximation. The frequency denominator is all letters in that treatment. A movement from 0.12 to 0.21 is about 9 percentage points, whereas its relative increase using those rounded numbers is about 75%; the two descriptions have different units. Exact ratios calculated from the raw counts need not equal ratios of the rounded displayed frequencies. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 32

The next histogram shows the distribution of positive donation amounts, conditional on giving. It uses a different denominator from the frequency table. A treatment can change how many recipients donate, the amounts donors give, or both. The conditional histogram alone cannot establish the change in average revenue per mailed letter. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 33

Timing and the revenue denominator

The source reports these CHF totals and Christmas means:

Outcome No gift Small gift Large gift
Christmas 2001 total 24,673 27,106 40,877
Christmas mean per letter 7.56 8.37 12.21
February 2002 total 14,023 13,206 13,165
Combined total 38,696 40,312 54,042

For example, 24,673/3,262 is about CHF7.56, so the mean is per letter, including recipients who gave nothing, rather than per positive donor. The slide footnote retains donations of at most CHF500 (approximately €350). The February totals are lower in the gift groups than in control, suggesting that timing or substitution must be considered; combined totals still remain higher for the large gift group. Revenue is not net profit: postcard, postage and other treatment costs are not supplied here, so these totals do not establish net returns. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 34

Bounded verification: the publisher abstract for Falk 2007, Econometrica 75(5), 1501–1511, confirms random assignment, approximately 10,000 letters, and the reported 17%/75% relative increases in giving frequency for small/large gifts. Full external paper access was not required for the lecture's reproduced tables and is not claimed here.

Relative pay and charitable gifts are core applications because they test social motivations outside anonymous laboratory games. The important skill is to reconstruct the comparison, prediction, outcome and limitation. The lecture's final summary reports social preferences as relevant in labour and donor contexts; it does not turn each empirical percentage into a universal behavioural constant. L3 BE_SP_field IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 35

sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
O012-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: In a hypothetical randomized charity mailing, no-gift and gift groups each receive 1000 letters. No-gift has 120 positive donors and gift 210. Christmas gross revenue is CHF 6000 versus CHF 10000; later revenue CHF 4000 versus CHF 3000. The gift accompanies the request before the donation decision. Compute response frequencies, the percentage-point and relative-percent change, Christmas average per letter versus per positive donor, combined average per letter, and incremental net return if extra gift cost is CHF 0.5 per gift-group letter and all other costs are identical. Explain what the conditional-positive histogram misses, why timing matters, and which reciprocity versus selfish/altruistic predictions require maintained information/preferences. Distinguish these supplied toy costs from the actual source’s missing net-cost data.

Complete solution and essential rubric: Frequencies are \(120/1000=0.12000000\) and \(210/1000=0.21000000\). Difference is \(9.00000000\) percentage points; relative rise is \((0.21/0.12-1)100=75.00000000\%\). Christmas means per letter are \(6000/1000=6.00000000\) and \(10000/1000=10.00000000\)CHF, including zeros; per positive donor they are \(6000/120=50.00000000\) and \(10000/210=47.61904762\)CHF. Combined gross per letter is \(10000/1000=10.00000000\) versus \(13000/1000=13.00000000\) CHF. Incremental net is \((13000-10000)-1000(0.5)=2500.00000000\) CHF under the hypothetical common-cost assumptions. A positive-donation histogram conditions on giving and cannot alone determine response probability or revenue/letter. Lower later giving can reflect timing/substitution, so Christmas alone is incomplete. Pure selfishness without another benefit predicts no giving; simple altruism alone need not vary with gift size if charity information/beliefs are fixed; reciprocity predicts a gift gradient, but attention/beliefs/warm glow can overlap. The actual Falk table totals 9,846 letters (roughly 10,000), uses counts/rounded frequency denominators and has no supplied treatment costs; its gross totals cannot prove actual net profitability. Gifts accompany solicitation, rather than preceding the request. These calculations are toy outputs, not observed donor results. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Required components: probability_and_mean_denominators, timing_and_incremental_net_return, conditional_predictions_and_design_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: Conditional-positive amounts equated with all-letter means; percentage points equated with relative rise; Christmas only used for full return; actual missing costs invented; gift-before-decision incorrectly becomes before solicitation.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. Every I/D form covers all components; W1, S1, the prerequisite and C1 are forbidden substitutes. A D form used for acquisition cannot later be counted again as delayed success. No teach-generated item may replace a named full check; additional verified explanation/practice is allowed under the unchanged method and may not fabricate evidence. If fewer than two fresh forms remain for acquisition, return a plan_issue for an additional prepared bank.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Social preferences in childhood; fingerprint e0a3559c498c69bafe1c4a6d41bffa0c3f527a21fdd89a26affaabf6a221d04b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Social preferences in childhood

Are preferences fixed traits, or can social experience shape them? This is separate from asking whether preferences are selfish: stable preferences could be other-regarding, and changing preferences could remain selfish. The lecture contrasts a traditional stability assumption, illustrated by Stigler and Becker (1977, p. 76), with a social-environment view attributed to Peter Hedström. Those positions motivate empirical questions rather than establish either answer by assertion. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 1–4

The map follows the framing, experimental design and results. The core foundation is to derive what each payoff comparison identifies before attaching a preference label to a child. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 2–16

Three games distinguish different motives

Fehr, Bernhard and Rockenbach (2008) use anonymous, one-shot allocations of sweets between a child and another child. The lecture describes approximately 250 Swiss children aged 3–8; the consulted Nature paper reports 229 analysed children, so the lecture's count is approximate rather than an exact sample size. Partners are either classmates from the same school/kindergarten (ingroup) or unknown children from another one (outgroup). The photo shows allocation cards and the group-photo cue identifying partner status; the child does not bargain face to face with the partner. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 6–7

Write a payoff as (own sweets, partner's sweets). The source's tasks are:

Game Available allocations What changes?
Costless prosocial/sharing \((1,1)\) or \((1,0)\) Own sweets stay fixed; helping the partner also removes advantageous inequality.
Costless envy \((1,1)\) or \((1,2)\) Own sweets stay fixed; equality conflicts with increasing the partner's payoff.
Costly sharing \((1,1)\) or \((2,0)\) Equality and helping the partner require sacrificing one own sweet.

A purely selfish child is indifferent between the two options in the first two games because own payoff is one in either case; selfishness does not strictly predict one tied option. In costly sharing, selfishness strictly predicts \((2,0)\). A strongly egalitarian child selects equality in all three; a sufficiently altruistic child selects the higher partner payoff, including accepting a cost to share. Spite instead favours reducing the other's payoff. Strength matters when own payoff must be sacrificed. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 6, 8–13

Read the whole choice pattern

The source table exhausts the eight combinations of two choices in three games:

Source classification Prosocial game Envy game Sharing game
Strongly egalitarian \((1,1)\) \((1,1)\) \((1,1)\)
Weakly egalitarian \((1,1)\) \((1,1)\) \((2,0)\)
Strongly generous \((1,1)\) \((1,2)\) \((1,1)\)
Weakly generous \((1,1)\) \((1,2)\) \((2,0)\)
Ambiguous type \((1,0)\) \((1,1)\) \((1,1)\)
Spiteful \((1,0)\) \((1,1)\) \((2,0)\)
Ambiguous type \((1,0)\) \((1,2)\) \((1,1)\)
Ambiguous type \((1,0)\) \((1,2)\) \((2,0)\)

These are the source's behavioural classifications, not infallible personality diagnoses. Because the selfish benchmark permits either costless choice, a child choosing \((2,0)\) in sharing could also produce several of these costless patterns without a strict selfish preference among them. One cannot identify a unique utility function from one tied choice. Consistency, understanding, context and measurement also matter. The four Sli.do pages ask students to predict inequality-averse, altruistic, spiteful and selfish choices; no poll results are supplied, so the reasoning above supplies model predictions rather than invented class responses. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 8–13

The age comparison is conditional on the partner group

The lecture's repeated age figure concerns ingroup partners. The proportion making the egalitarian choice in costly sharing rises from about 9% at ages 3–4 to about 22% at 5–6 and 45% at 7–8. The costless prosocial and envy choices reach roughly 78% and 80% at 7–8. These graphical readings show why the lecture describes young children as mostly selfish and older children as more egalitarian, but the costless-game ties mean that label should not be treated as direct proof of a unique motive for every young child. Even among the oldest group, fewer than half choose costly equality. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 14–15

This is a cross-sectional age comparison, not a panel following the same children as they grow. It supports an age-related pattern, not a causal estimate of ageing or a particular upbringing. Its ingroup caption also prevents generalizing the displayed percentages to unknown outgroup children. The lecture's statement that later development includes efficiency concerns and altruism is attributed only to unspecified “different studies”; no unprovided later-age evidence or effect size is certified here. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 14–16

Bounded primary check: Fehr, Bernhard and Rockenbach, “Egalitarianism in young children,” Nature 454 (2008), 1079–1083, publisher proof, physical pp. 1–2 and methods on p. 6, verifies the three tasks, sample count, anonymous one-shot design and ingroup interpretation. The proof distinguishes costless choices from costly sharing; numerical source figures remain tied to their displayed partner condition. This is supporting verification, not ingestion of the paper's entire additional outgroup analysis.

The next question is whether family background is merely associated with preferences or whether changing a child's social environment can alter measured prosociality. Distinguishing those two claims is the foundation of the mentoring application. L4 BE_formation IES 2026.pdf, physical PDF pp. 16–18 Social Environment and Mentoring

A hypothetical child chooses \([(1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 1)]\) in that order. In the third, selecting \((1,1)\) costs one own sweet relative to \((2,0)\). Pure self-interest is indifferent over the first two pairs and strictly prefers \((2,0)\) in sharing. It compares different children by age, not a panel or randomized upbringing, so neither causal ageing nor a universal outgroup pattern follows. sections.title: Outcome and conditions

sections.html:
Check the prerequisites
  • O001 outcome and repair route: the experimental intervention/control contrast is distinct from a background association.
  • O013 outcome and repair route: allocation patterns and tied choices limit one-to-one preference interpretations. The trust-survey and observer-rating distinctions are taught in the included O014 foundation below, before its diagnostic or assessed forms.

Included O014 measurement and index foundation

Read this bounded foundation before O014-P1 and the worked example. The checked passage “What “prosociality” measures” below distinguishes an incentivized dictator allocation (a choice), a trust survey (stated beliefs about others’ trustworthiness, intentions or reliability), and a mother rating (an observer questionnaire). These are different measurements; neither a choice nor a stated belief uniquely identifies every social preference. O013 supplies allocation-pattern and tie reasoning, not the trust-survey distinction. If the measurement part of P1 fails, repair it here and in that complete included checked passage; repair random-assignment reasoning through O001.

For the hypothetical arithmetic in this lesson, let \(z_A,z_T,z_M\) denote the three component scores after each component has been standardized. Define the mean-component-z index as \(J=(z_A+z_T+z_M)/3\). Its treatment-minus-control contrast is the arithmetic mean of the three supplied component contrasts. Report that contrast and any supplied benchmark gap in the same mean-component-z index units. Standardizing the components does not give their average a standard deviation of one: the average’s variance depends on their variances and covariances. A subsequently standardized composite would instead require the composite’s own reference mean and standard deviation, for example \(Z_J=(J-\mu_J)/\sigma_J\) with \(\sigma_J>0\). Those reference quantities are not supplied, so no composite-SD conversion is requested or inferred. This is a transparent explanation of the toy index definition, not a re-estimate of the study’s empirical effect.

O014-P1, item_version 1, prerequisite_diagnostic. Prompt: What does random assignment compare, and why is a dictator allocation not identical to a survey statement about trusting others?

Complete key and rubric: Random assignment compares assigned intervention/control under its design, not automatically every background difference (O001). An incentivized allocation measures a choice while a trust statement records a belief; neither uniquely identifies every social preference (included O014 measurement foundation and the complete “What “prosociality” measures” passage below). Require both; repair O001 for assignment reasoning and the included O014 foundation for measurement, before retrying. Pass requires every requested reason and result; partial for an omitted reason or unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This diagnostic never counts as acquisition. Current or explicitly compatible committed independent prerequisite evidence may permit skipping its check; familiarity alone cannot. Use the cited complete prerequisite lesson or the named included foundation, then the worked example, after a partial/failing entry check.
